records.text: US Economic Perspectives 16 October 2026 ab 2 Fiscal deadlines and debt ceiling debates Fiscal negotiations have the potential to become more fractious. FY 2027 funding and the roughly $500 billion surface transportation bill expire on December 11, making a short-term extension into 2027 plausible. A subsequent deal could pair higher defense spending sought by Republicans with higher non-defense spending sought by Democrats, while softening some Medicaid savings already in law. The debt ceiling could provide another bargaining point. Democrats could seek changes to Medicaid provisions, housing incentives, clean-energy credits, and other domestic priorities in exchange for their votes. The eventual agreement could therefore be stimulative and leave deficits wider than the CBO baseline, even if divided government rules out a large partisan package. The path to a deal would also raise shutdown and debt-ceiling risks. records.text: European Equity Strategy 16 October 2026 ab 7 Expectations and share prices The earnings hurdle differs from the market hurdle Expected growth alone is not a sufficient guide to earnings risk. Companies whose estimates, valuations and share prices have already risen face a higher market hurdle, even if their fundamental outlook remains strong. Conversely, substantial derating may reduce the threshold for a positive response, although a lower valuation does not itself constitute evidence of an earnings recovery. The most informative cases are those where prices and estimates have diverged. Positive revisions without a comparable price response may indicate under-recognised improvement. Price appreciation accompanied by weaker estimates leaves less protection if results fail to validate expectations. GDP growth above expectations : China’s Q3 GDP grew by 4.5% y/y, accelerating from a 4.3% y/y rise in Q2. This print outpaced both our estimate of 4.3% and the market consensus of 4.4%. China’s industrial production growth picked up to 5.5% y/y in September, from 4.5% in July and 5.2% in August. This indicates that weather-related disruptions from early Q3 have subsided, and that there was a marginal lift from accelerated fiscal spending. Moreover, service output accelerated to 4.8% y/y in September, up from 4.3% in July and 4.1% in August. With YTD growth at 4.6% y/y, the economy needs only 4.2% growth in Q4 to meet the annual target of 4.5–5.0%. Achieving this target should be manageable, in our view, as the base effect becomes more favourable in Q4. Last year’s Q4 GDP growth of 4.5% marked the annual low. Domestic demand especially is supported by low comparables: retail sales growth slowed from 4.5% y/y in 9M25 to 1.6% y/y in Q4 2025. European sovereign risk is back in focus as fiscal concerns have pushed French n spreads to decade highs and tentative spillovers have emerged in other markets, including Italy. With this raising the question of whether the Euro area could face a renewed debt crisis, we compare today’s conditions with the 2011-15 episode. We see several similarities. Fiscal imbalances are elevated (with further spending n pressures from defence and ageing), interest rates are high and rising, and debt dynamics look concerning in several countries (including France, Belgium, Austria and Finland). Financial-market vulnerabilities also persist through sovereign exposures and non-bank leverage, while greater political fragmentation complicates the fiscal adjustment required. But today’s starting point is stronger in several important respects. Real and n nominal growth are materially higher, household finances are more robust, external imbalances and reliance on foreign financing are smaller, and banks— especially in Southern Europe—have healthier capital, asset quality and profitability. The Euro area has also strengthened its institutional architecture through the ESM, greater common EU issuance and ECB tools to address fragmentation risk. As a result, the risks of disorderly market escalation and real economy contagion n look notably lower. records.text: European Rates Strategy 16 October 2026 ab 3 What if a member state fails to pay? The legal framework also provides safeguards if a member fails to pay. For NGEU, Article 9 of the 2020 Own Resources Decision allows the Commission, within specified limits, to call additional resources from other members if one fails to honour a call, while the non-paying member remains liable. Together with Article 14 of the 2014 Making Available Regulation and Articles 311 and 323 TFEU, these provisions lead Moody’s to view the framework as the equivalent of joint-and-several support, although the mechanism has never been tested. This is not a direct guarantee from member states to bondholders, whose claim remains against the EU. How much does France matter? Our calculations suggest that, all else equal, France would have to fall to Baa3 under Moody’s and BBB under S&P before a French downgrade alone lowered their respective weighted-average member assessments; France is outside Fitch’s AAA support pool . Rating developments elsewhere provide an additional buffer. Under S&P, countries on positive outlook account for 16% of EU GDP, compared with 5% on negative outlook. This gap can persist due to technical/global factors and if political factors keep spreads elevated. It is also possible, however, that r will moderate again if it has been pushed up by growth optimism larger than the likely pickup in longer-term growth trends, or that g picks up more significantly due to AI-related productivity gains. Either way, both a modestly lower r and a higher g would reduce some of the required fiscal adjust- ments. This would not, however, remove it altogether in countries running large primary budget deficits. records.text: US Economics Weekly 16 October 2026 ab 6 Underappreciated midterm risks Based on the most recent polling, the midterm elections are likely to increase Democratic control of Congress. Democrats need a net gain of three House seats, and the incumbent president's party has lost an average of 24 seats over the past 20 midterm cycles. A Democratic House would make gridlock and fiscal brinkmanship more likely; a Democratic sweep could also affect monetary policy through increased control of the Senate confirmation process. If the Democrats win control of the Senate, we would expect as many as four of the current members of the Board of Governors depart in 2027 or by early 2028. Spillovers into monetary policymaking: an underappreciated risk A blue sweep could have implications for the Congressional confirmation process. Natural turnover in the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve gives the administration the ability to appoint new members. Those new members must go through a Congressional confirmation process. A Democratic majority could therefore constrain the administration’s ability to secure confirmation for its preferred nominees. Greater Democratic influence over confirmations, alongside increased oversight, could in turn provide the FOMC with a degree of additional institutional insulation. Based on our balance calculations, these volumes appear achievable, particularly as Russian domestic diesel demand typically declines substantially during the winter months. If refinery runs recover to 4 mbd in January, still 1.2 mbd below their 2025 average, Russia could potentially export up to 300 kbd of diesel during the winter. If runs stay at 3.6 mbd rather than recovering to 4 mbd, export potential in early 2027 would fall to roughly 150 kbd. Brazil: About stocks, not flows Brazil stands out for the largest rise in real long-end yields since 2019, far exceeding that implied by its fiscal-monetary r-star gap. Unlike most countries, its declining FM gap has been driven largely by rising long-run debt expectations (Exhibit 11), rather than the primary balance, which has been broadly flat since 2016. The current adminstration has been quick to approve transactions making it a favorable deal environment. We note that some management teams do note that the prior administration was not as supportive of bank mergers and thus the deal approval process was lengthy and in some cases difficult to overcome. Some federal agencies, like the CFPB, have become less active in the current administration. A Blue Wave could make such agencies take a more active role and thus result in more consumer protection laws, deposit sweeps or limiting credit card late fees. The trend over the last few years has been less regulation, fines, and protectionism which has resulted in loan growth, increased profitability and returns. Thus, the market could be very sensitive to increased regulation, especially by the CFPB. records.text: infrastructure demand grows around 7% this year (vs ~10% prev.). Growth is also held back by continued weakness in property and by renewables demand falling from last year’s record installations. We expect growth in China end-use demand to recover to ~1% in 2027 as these drags ease. A bright spot is data centers, where we raise our demand forecast across our forecast horizon, offsetting weakness elsewhere (Exhibit 10). We raise our global datacenter copper demand forecast by around 125kt in 2026 and 180kt in 2027, to around 550kt and 700kt respectively. This reflects higher global capacity estimates from our US equity research team, combined with regional forecasts for China and broader regional coverage (ASEAN, Australia). Our equity analysts see capacity estimates as potentially conservative relative to expected investment, with AI/cloud company capex projected to reach around $1.2tn by 2030. Beyond 2027, visibility over new projects is more limited, and announced capacity additions decline towards the end of the decade. We therefore supplement the announced project pipeline with an allowance for unannounced capacity, informed by the GS datacenter capex tracker. We incorporate only half the gap between announced additions and the path implied by capex growth, reflecting uncertainty over the conversion of spending into capacity and constraints on power, equipment and permitting. Direct policy actions from either side are more likely aimed at participants further down the supply chain and have historically failed to materially impact industry fundamentals. We previously focused on tariffs and trade measures back in 2024 when we wrote about economic proposals and potential impacts to Chemicals under both a Harris administration and a Trump administration. The tariff regime implemented by the Trump Administration following the 2024 election accelerated the pace and magnitude of reactionary measures by trade counterparties just as chemicals fundamentals were attempting to rebound. A small group of variables explain a large share of the variation Looking at the performance of our model, we find that both the 5-year CDS and the USD spread model specifications can explain EM sovereign spread changes well, with R-squared coefficients in a high 60-80% range for a large share of sovereigns for the CDS model (Exhibit 9), and a slightly lower but still high 50-60%+ range for the USD spread model (Exhibit 10). Overall, both models seem to perform better for EM IG sovereigns, with poorer performance particularly for B-rated and Frontier sovereigns, such as Egypt, Turkiye (Exhibit 9), Ghana and Pakistan (Exhibit 10). This is consistent with the orthogonal property of Frontier trades, whose fluctuations tend to be less correlated to global risk and more idiosyncratic than their EM HY counterparts. Turning to the optimal variable selection process, we find that a small number of global factors can explain the bulk of the variation of EM 5-year CDS and USD bond spreads, in line with the literature and our choice to optimise for three variables only. Investor concerns over AI equity valuations and debt sustainability drove global equities lower (KOSPI lost 7% in one day) and resulted in a flight to safety via global government bonds. Odds of another hike at the October FOMC meeting further moderated after a speech from Chair Warsh at the IMF’s annual meeting in Bangkok. The reaction was driven less by what Warsh said than what he did not say. As expected, Warsh stuck to his preference of not giving forward guidance and reiterated the central bank’s goal of delivering price stability. Howev- er, the OIS repricing post-speech suggests that investors were hoping the FOMC Chair would comment on the hotter-than-expected CPI reading. Core PCE could plausibly end the year at 3.4%, especially since the booming nominal economy increases the risks that the energy shock will get passed through. Most of the FOMC was on board with two hikes this year. Why not do the second one in Oct, to retain the optionality for a third in Dec? Markets are testing the Fed’s pain threshold Markets briefly priced more than a 50% chance of an Oct hike soon after the Sep CPI print, but then retraced due to AI concerns. Stepping back though, the NASDAQ is only about 5% off its all-time high and credit spreads – even high yield – aren’t particularly wide by historical standards. So markets are assuming the Fed’s pain threshold is very low. These floaters are priced at par with their coupons resetting periodically to SOFR plus a margin, and thus have more limited price sensitivity than regular fixed rate bonds. However, in a large rate selloff scenario, floaters are still vulnerable to extension risk and hitting the cap, at which point they start to behave like fixed rate bonds. The recently introduced VADM and Z bonds, as well as NAS classes, help combat this. As a reminder, a Very Accurately Determined Maturity or VADM bond is designed to pro- vide protection against extension risk. VADM bond cashflows are derived from the interest accrued and deferred on the Z bond, so the two are always structured together. VADMs can provide a guaranteed final date for the receipt of principal and a maximum weighted average life even if prepayments drop to zero. This has value for investors looking for certainty around final return of principal. Meanwhile, the Z bond only begins amortizing after the VADM is paid off (Figure 16V A D M b o n d s a r e d e s i g n e d t o p r o v i d e p r o t e c t i o n a g a i n s t e x t e n s i o n r i s k t h r o u g h c a s h f l o w s d e r i v e d f r o m t h e i n t e r e s t a c c r u e d a n d d e f e r r e d o n t h e Z b o n d ). In the recently issued CHASE and JPMMT deals, these VADM and Z classes are the A19 and A20 classes that are a sequential split of the A5 25% LCF.

Fitch assigns EIB a aaa standalone credit profile; shareholder support, based on the average rating of key shareholders Germany, France and Italy, is only a+ and therefore provides no uplift. S&P similarly rates EIB AAA on its own extremely strong enterprise and financial risk profiles and does not currently factor extraordinary shareholder support into the rating; callable capital from AAA shareholders instead provides an additional buffer if capitalisation deteriorates. Moody’s gives shareholder support a greater role, using an A1 weighted-average shareholder rating based on subscribed-capital shares, alongside “Very High” willingness to support. France therefore has a sizeable weight in this metric. Our calculations suggest that, all else equal, France would have to fall to Baa2 before its deterioration alone lowered the weighted-average shareholder rating. However, Moody’s already assesses EIB’s intrinsic financial strength at aaa, supported by its capital, asset quality, funding, central-bank liquidity access and governance. Shareholder support is also underpinned by legally enforceable callable-capital commitments. The obligation to meet a capital call is embedded in the EIB Statute, which forms part of the EU Treaties. Based on BDC filings, ~21% of US private credit debt matures over the next two years, vs. ~15% in US LL and ~14% in EU LL, where near-term maturities are already at cycle highs. The maturity wall is broad-based but most pronounced in healthcare, energy and materials, with 7%, 11% and 7% of each sector’s outstanding debt maturing, respectively. While healthcare and materials could face mild refinancing pressure amid sector-specific weakness, energy appears lower risk given recent tailwinds. Technology, where capital-market access is likely most vulnerable, has more runway, with limited refinancing pressure until Q2’27. Risks rise materially thereafter, however, with ~21% of outstanding technology debt maturing by end-2028. In our view, the Q1’27 runway could limit near-term headline volatility in technology and software credit, but does not resolve the underlying risk from AI disruption. Upcoming maturities should act as a forcing mechanism, requiring stress in individual software credits to be addressed. The 2027-28 refinancing cycle could also coincide with a less accommodative funding backdrop: direct-lending volumes are down ~50%/~17% YTD in the US/EU, respectively, while redemption requests remain elevated across the broader private-credit ecosystem. records.text: Mine supply weakens further in 2026, with a recovery expected in 2027 We lower our 2026 mine supply forecast by a further 100kt relative to our prior estimates and now expect a 0.8% year-on-year decline. The revision mainly reflects weaker output in Chile, where we now expect production to fall 7% (vs 6% previously). This adds to the outages at Grasberg in Indonesia and Kamoa-Kakula in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which together accounted for around 60% of our earlier 2026 350kt mine supply downgrade and remain the main drivers of this year’s global decline. We expect production at both operations to recover gradually in 2027, but neither to return to full capacity until 2028. Chilean production fell 13% year-on-year in August, taking the year-to-date year-over-year decline to 8% (Exhibit 13). Lower grades and deferred maintenance have weighed on output, while severe winter storms disrupted operations and power infrastructure, prompting guidance cuts at Los Pelambres and Caserones. We expect the immediate weather effects to be temporary, but labour negotiations and further weather disruption remain downside risks. A super El Niño could extend weather disruption in Chile and bring heavy rains to Peru in early 2027, while a return to dry conditions in southern Africa could constrain hydropower availability and copper production. records.text: However, cathode-based rod output rose by around 305kt (+4%), offsetting around half of the decline, while total rod output is down only around 4% YTD. Higher cathode use therefore raises refined copper requirements without implying stronger underlying consumption: lower direct scrap use accounts for almost all of the increase in China’s refined copper demand this year (Exhibit 5). We expect the disruption to persist into 2027, with direct-use scrap consumption falling 27% in 2026 and declining further next year. Recent fieldwork from our China equity research team suggests that roughly 500kt of annual domestic scrap flow (around 18% of normal domestic scrap supply) may currently be impaired, with risks of further deterioration in 2027. Resolving the underlying invoicing bottleneck is likely to require a broader restructuring of the collection chain, away from small, single-metal operators towards larger and more diversified recycling platforms. Given stronger real growth and higher inflation, nominal GDP growth now is markedly firmer than during the “lowflation” period of 2011-2015. Current account deficits now are notably lower compared to the run-up to the debt crisis (especially in Spain, Portugal and Italy), pointing to reduced dependence on foreign financing and limited risks of sudden stops in capital flows. Although weaker deal volumes do not necessarily indicate a shortage of capital, the combination could make lenders more selective as refinancing needs rise. We therefore expect increasingly bifurcated outcomes from Q2’27, with weaker technology credits facing higher spreads, tighter terms or restructuring as maturities accelerate. Weaker vintages compound maturity risk Private credit’s refinancing risk is greater than what maturity walls alone suggest. Around half of USD private debt maturing over the next two years (~11% of the total universe) is “high risk”, being either loans from weaker vintages with elevated non- accrual rates, software, or both. Across all BDC vintages since COVID, non-accrual rates are the highest for the 2020-21 vintages at 11% and 8%, respectively. These weaker- quality vintages are also the ones approaching maturity first: ~33% of 2020-vintage debt matures before 2028, which drops to ~19% for 2021 and ~12% for 2022. As a result, the near-term maturity wall appears heavily skewed toward lower-quality debt and software, with ~37% of private debt maturing in 2027-28 coming from the lower- quality 2020-21 vintages and an additional ~16% coming from technology/software This report has been prepared by UBS AG London Branch. records.text: argued tighter financial conditions were doing some of the ECB’s job for it. On the fiscal front, last week’s EU summit did not yield any breakthrough on the next EU budget. The rejection of Ireland’s proposed EUR141bn cut to the Multiannual Financial Framework underscores a lack of consensus, leaving president Antonio Costa to seek compromise ahead of the 26 November summit. Such a compromise looks increasingly challenging given domestic political uncertainty in a number of key member states. In France, we note that Rassemblement National – ahead in the latest polling for the April presidential election – has pledged to cut France’s contribution to the EU budget should it win. There appears to be more consensus on a tougher stance toward China, and the recent agreement of a cap on imports of hybrid vehicles suggests diplomatic solutions can still be found. That said, this does not solve underlying competitiveness issues, for which we think more progress on implementing aspects of the Draghi and Letta reports is key. In the meantime, the outcome of Moody’s credit rating review of France will land on Friday. Given the negative outlook, worse-than-expected growth data and rising pressure on the deficit, a rating downgrade to A1 (stable outlook) seems more likely than not. This would also equalize Moody’s rating with S&P and Fitch , who already rate France at A+. The original bill had broad support in the Senate but House amendments could mean less Senate support for the revised legislation, see here. Fiscal, Fed, and oversight Oversight would intensify for the administration's disbursement of funds, regulation, and tariff policy. At the same time, the administration would retain substantial executive authority over targeted tariffs and trade investigations, energy and banking deregulation, drug pricing, housing initiatives, and foreign-investment announcements. The result would be a mix of gridlock, negotiated fiscal expansion, selective bipartisan deals, and continued unilateral action, with the Fed confirmation channel an important, and underappreciated, link between the election and the macro outlook. For the macro outlook, the key takeaway is that the election could change not only the amount and composition of fiscal support, but also the institutional setting for monetary policy. Markets may focus first on shutdown risk and the prospect of wider deficits, but the Senate's role in shaping the Federal Reserve Board could prove more durable: a Democratic majority could limit the administration's ability to install nominees, reinforcing a focus on the Fed's independence, while increasing uncertainty around the future composition and reaction function of the FOMC.

Morgan, Intex The Non-accelerated Senior or NAS class aims to reduce prepayment risk for the investor through a different structure. NAS classes have a lockout period for the first several years where they receive only interest payments and no unscheduled principal. During the lockout period, the NAS class is insulated from prepayments. Once this ends, they start receiving a percentage of the total principal proportional to the share of NAS UPB out of a specified total UPB. The smaller the NAS class share, the more buffer there is against prepayments. M Idea 10 Financial conditions: The Fed awakens Following the 25bp rate hike in September and the shift into an "oil risk premium" baseline, we reset our financial conditions index to September 15, 2026, the day prior to the September FOMC meeting, to track our FRB/US-based measure of financial conditions in this new hiking cycle. As of the October 15th market close, financial conditions were 26bp tighter than they were before the September FOMC meeting. The index aims to capture how changes in asset prices weigh on future economic activity. It includes five daily variables: the 10-year Treasury yield, S&P 500 returns, the corporate BBB credit spread, the valuation of the U.S. dollar, and the price of oil. These are aggregated based on their estimated growth elasticities relative to the federal funds rate using the Federal Reserve's FRB/US model. As a result, the index can be interpreted as the equivalent change in the federal funds rate, expressed in basis points, required to generate a similar effect on economic activity. From the day before the September FOMC meeting until October 15, the tightening in financial conditions has been equivalent to about a 26bp hike in the federal funds rate, reflecting dollar appreciation and a net rise in the 10-year Treasury yield. The FCI had been tighter a week earlier, on October 8; and it tightened further through most of this week, until it reversed course with a drop in 10-year Treasury yields on October 15. records.text: 38 Tarek HamidAC (1-212) 834-5468 tarek.x.hamid@jpmorgan.com North America Credit Research 16 October 2026 J P M O R G A N HG & HY Paper/Packaging Global packaging companies are impacted by movements in the US Dollar (notably against the Euro) given the high degree of international asset exposure in the space. As we noted in our Metals/Mining writeup, we expect elevated yields in a Republican legislative government to be beneficial to the USD, while de-escalation and reduced funding in a Democratic legislative scenario could be moderating for the USD. Under a Republican Congress, inflationary policies, further support around tariffs and a potential Fed hiking cycle could keep rates higher for longer and support the dollar near term, though fiscal concerns could weigh on the dollar over time. Energy input costs and inflationary pass throughs remain a focus in packaging heading into midterm elections. The administration is already targeting pump prices through executive action. It has authorized Russian diesel imports through April 7, 2027 and expanded highway use of tax-exempt dyed diesel. Under a Republican Congress, we expect that focus to continue, including the President's floated federal gas tax suspension. Under a divided government, we expect more focus on electricity costs, including requiring data centers to pay the full cost of the grid upgrades they need. Under either outcome, global supply remains the main driver of fuel prices. Before the conflict with Iran began

records.text: Please ref er to important inf ormation at the end of the report and MAR disclosures China: Stronger-than-expected Q3 growth rules out additional stimulus OUR KEY VIEWS ▪ We believe that China will not require further stimulus measures in Q4 as Q3 GDP growth has exceeded expectations. ▪ We expect the recovery to continue in Q4, and maintain our full-year GDP growth forecast at 4.6%. GDP growth above expectations : China’s Q3 GDP grew by 4.5% y/y, accelerating from a 4.3% y/y rise in Q2. This print outpaced both our estimate of 4.3% and the market consensus of 4.4%. China’s industrial production growth picked up to 5.5% y/y in September, from 4.5% in July and 5.2% in August. This indicates that weather-related disruptions from early Q3 have subsided, and that there was a marginal lift from accelerated fiscal spending. Moreover, service output accelerated to 4.8% y/y in September, up from 4.3% in July and 4.1% in August. With YTD growth at 4.6% y/y, the economy needs only 4.2% growth in Q4 to meet the annual target of 4.5–5.0%. Achieving this target should be manageable, in our view, as the base effect becomes more favourable in Q4. Last year’s Q4 GDP growth of 4.5% marked the annual low. Domestic demand especially is supported by low comparables: retail sales growth slowed from 4.5% y/y in 9M25 to 1.6% y/y in Q4 2025. records.text: 16 October 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Deutsche Bank AG Page 2 continues to push higher, with IT equipment rising further to 2% YoY, the highest level on record. Evidence of indirect energy effects continues to remain limited. Our high energy-intensive index has risen back to its July levels (3.0%), but as this largely reflects the movement in travel-related components, we read it more as seasonal noise than a clear signal of broadening price pressures. Our domestic inflation indicator holding steady at 3.5%, reinforces this view. Euro area August IP Euro area industrial production fell 0.5% m/m in August. This headline included a sharp 3.1% m/m decline in Irish production; excluding Ireland, the fall in activity is lower by 0.3% m/m. At the country level, industrial activity exhibited widespread softness during August. Output contracted across almost all major member states: Italian production fell sharply by 1.3% m/m, Spanish output declined by 0.7% m/m, and France recorded a 0.3% m/ m. This broad -based contraction underscores the persistent cyclical and structural headwinds facing European manufacturing, leaving the region's industrial sector on a highly fragile footing. Germany was the sole outlier, with headline production surging by 2.0% m/m to an 18-month high. However, this spike was overwhelmingly driven by a massive 9.3% m/m jump in construction, which was fuelled by a unique one -off completion of a major battery storage infrastructure project in Leuna. We expect the relief to be cancelled over the long term, even though it may be kept for 2027. Either way, we do not see it as a game changer for HGB demand. As structured in 2025 and 2026, the relief gave local banks a strong incentive to add HGBs towards year-end. This is visible in the holdings data (Figure 14) and has driven the seasonal collapse in asset swap spreads around November and December. Terms of Trade & FX As a brief refresher, the theory behind the link between terms of trade and exchange rates comes from two early academic papers, Harberger (1950)[1] and Laursen & Metzler (1950)[2]. The idea is that when the balance of payments (BoP) is pushed into disequilibrium, either through deterioration or an improvement in the current account resulting from a shift in terms of trade, the real exchange rate should adjust to offset pressures on the BoP . Given this theoretical relationship between terms of trade and FX, we constructed our daily indices with two primary goals in mind: i) to track shifts in commodity prices and their directional impact on the balance of payments for each economy on a high-frequency basis, and ii) to offer a simple framework for assessing the potential implications of a commodity price shock (or outlook) on an economy and its currency. records.text: to global factors that are raising yields. Here too the framework provides guidance. The framework implements the stance but doesn’t interfere with it. The stance itself is set by the policy rate (deposit facility rate). Indeed, the most recent account notes that the repricing of long-end yields “ could have implications for appropriate policy rates in the future”. It does not say it has implications for the path of portfolio run -off. Given the gradual and well communicated pace of run -off, a pause risks causing more confusion around how and when to restart. In terms of the market reaction so far, t he macro FCI peaked on the 29 th of September. The sovereign spread component has risen but is offset by lower nominal yields. As highlighted here, terminal rate pricing has also declined, indicating that the market is already doing some of the adjustment via monetary policy expectations. In addition, our free float framework suggests term premium is more global than local, and merely pausing or stopping QT would have a limited effect on yields. The other angle to questions around stopping QT is whether this can be used to address fragmentation risks – namely to focus reinvestments on a single country. Using PEPP would involve a two -step decision – to pause run -offs, and then to refocus reinvestments on a single sovereign. It is debatable whether re-launching a tool created in response to the pandemic w ould stand up to scrutiny. It would also raise questions around hierarchy

Special Focus: Not many downgrades among the largest issuers YTD There is increasing investor concern around the potential ratings impact of surging HG issu- ance. In order to examine this, below we look at the YTD ratings changes for all HG issuers that have seen their net index debt grow by at least $10bn (17 issuers total fit this criteria). Needless to say, issuance has been highly concentrated in the AI buildout participants but there are also other unrelated issuers growing debt rapidly for other reasons, like M&A: Amazon and Alphabet alone added $94.5bn, while Salesforce, NVIDIA, Meta and Oracle each added more than $20bn. Rating outcomes have been mixed: NVIDIA improved, while Salesforce, Oracle, Abbott and Sysco were downgraded at one or more agencies. Of the 17 issuers that fit our screen, 12 are seasoned issuers of which 17% were upgraded, 33% downgraded and 50% have unchanged ratings. Five more were debut issuers, mainly data centers, and on balance that new debt was primarily in the A ratings category. Still, half of comparable large issuers were unchanged, suggesting the increase in debt has not yet produced broad ratings pressure.

The week of Oct 5 was relatively light on events, and yields inched lower over its course. The week of Oct 13 started off with several bank earnings calls on Tuesday and more in the following days. Wednesday’s CPI drew sharp intraday repricing across multiple asset classes. Concerns over AI valuations flared up later in the week. records.text: ABS Outlook for consumer credit is stronger than consumer sentiment indicators would suggest The recent release of the University of Michigan’s consumer confidence survey shows that consumers’ views of economic conditions are close to all-time lows (Exhibit 7). The Conference Board’s survey fared slightly better, but still shows low sentiment, the likes of which have not been seen since the immediate aftermath of the Global Financial Crisis. Our economists have argued that the large declines in consumer confidence can largely be explained by declines in confidence regarding US institutions rather than a literal summary of economic expectations. This conclusion offers comfort when assessing the financial strength of the consumer as we find the health to be disconnected from the sentiment. Various types of non-mortgage related consumer debt are currently reporting stable but elevated transition rates into newly delinquent territory (Exhibit 8). In order to ascertain where delinquency transition rates might go from here, we must first understand what delinquency transition rates have looked like during prior periods of weak or strong real income growth. Specifically, we pay the most attention to income growth in the three lowest income buckets, namely earners at the 60th percentile and below. Given the regime shift in German fiscal policy in 2025, as well as other sovereign risk reduction programs (TPI, NGEU) we add a dummy in the model to account for this increase in Bund risk premium. Our estimates imply that the rise in macro uncertainty has contributed to higher term premium in all major markets. This is consistent with not only the wider distribution around interest rates but also the series of supply shocks since the pandemic. CXMT’s move toward 4F² can also be viewed as a response to China’s constraints on conventional DRAM scaling. Restricted access to advanced lithography equipment, particularly EUV from ASML, makes it more challenging to reduce the minimum feature size, F. Moving from 6F² to 4F² offers another route to higher density: reducing the area required for each memory cell without relying entirely on finer lithography. However, 4F² does not only come with benefits. 4F² architecture’s smaller memory cells are more complex to manufacture, as vertical transistors must be built consistently, capacitors must still store enough charge in a smaller footprint, and closely packed wires should be precisely designed so that they don’t interfere with one another. Hybrid bonding adds further processing steps and requires precise alignment between the memory and control-circuit layers. These challenges can increase manufacturing costs and reduce yields, potentially offsetting the benefit of fitting more memory into the same area. 4F2 progress/comments by each major player However, CXMT is not the only player to prepare for next generation DRAM architecture. Morgan Core CPI Core PCE, /w forecast While recent Fedspeak is consistent with a hold in October, and we don’t expect a hike until December, it is worth considering the case for an immediate hike given the unflattering inflation data. The key rationale would be if there is little new information that we will learn in the next couple of months that would create a case for keeping rates on hold. This is especially convincing if one believes core inflation is persistently stuck near 3%, and that only a material slowdown in aggregate demand will knock inflation back toward 2%. Even if one doesn’t believe this, there is an argument to be made that the next two employment and inflation reports are unlikely to surprise in a way that will stop the FOMC from hiking in December. For example, weekly claims and ADP data already point towards the possibili- ty of a solid October jobs report. Meanwhile, business surveys, pass-through from energy costs, and import prices all suggest that core inflation could remain firm in the near term. A number of Fed speakers, however, have emphasized patience, and we think many mem- bers of the FOMC maintain a view that inflation is largely above target owing to a temporary series of shocks that will fade over time, particularly from energy and technology prices. To address this question, we examine the changes in 1M expiry swaption implied volatility in the first week of October (when the midterms rolled into the expiry window) in relation to 2-week expiry swaption implieds (for which the midterms remain outside the option win- dow). This allows us to infer the midterm premium currently priced into swaptions. We start by estimating the beta between 1M expiry implied vols and 2W expiry implied vols, which was 0.8 at the beginning of October for 10-year tails. This beta, taken together with the daily change in 2Wx10Y implied volatility, gives an expected change in 1Mx10Y implied volatility. We then compare the actual day-over-day changes with this expected change. As can be seen in Figure 12, this beta has been positive in every sector, around 0.2 bp/day. The global fiscal-monetary r-star gap, our preferred estimate of fiscal-monetary tensions, continued to widen into Q4 2026 across both developed and emerging markets (Exhibit 2). This measure uses IMF WEO vintages to compare a market's fiscal r-star (the real interest rate required to stabilize debt given prevailing primary deficits and inflation targets) with its monetary r-star (the economy's equilibrium real rate consistent with inflation at target). The gap between the two measures captures how much monetary tightening can be sustained before it begins to conflict with fiscal objectives by raising debt burdens, constraining public spending, or generating inflationary pressures (for more details, see: GEMs Viewpoint: Navigating budget storms: fiscal r-star 24 February 2025). We believe issuance activity remains on track to end the year in line with our estimate at $1,300 billion and $210 billion for gross and net issuance, respectively. Not surprisingly, issuance forecasts for 2027 are highly sensitive to the level and path of mortgage rates. Our economists’ and rates strategists’ currently forecast just one additional Fed hike (in December) and for 10-year Treasury yields to decline to 4.40% by year-end 2027, respectively. Consistent with these forecasts, our base case assumes that mortgage rates can decline to 6.40% by year-end 2027, with an average for the year around 6.65%. We also consider a scenario where mortgage rates average 7% in 2027. In our base case, we expect gross and net issuance to reach $1,200 billion and $185 billion, in 2027 (Exhibit 1). We expect a modest decline in the securitization rate, as discussed below. Under the 7.0% mortgage rate scenario, gross and net issuance could reach $1,100 billion and $165 billion. We expect home purchase loan issuance volumes to reach $875 billion in 2027 in our base case, a modest decline from 2026 volumes. The midterm results shouldn’t have a material impact on tariffs since they run through the executive and the courts, not the next Congress, but it remains a key focus for us — tariffs are bad for the consumer and volatility in policy makes it difficult for retailers and consumer companies to plan their business. The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on February 20, 2026, holding that the statute does not authorize presidential tariffs. With refunds phasing through CBP in April 2026, importers of record (including many of our retailers and consumer products companies) had claimed >$94bn by early June 2026. We treat the refund as a one- time cash item, not a structural tailwind, and find that most of our coverage is either using them to enhance their value message (i.e. discounting — WMT) or to pay down debt (for the more highly levered — KSS, MIK). We could see tariff increases from here; the administration has worked to backfill IEEPA revenue through more durable statutory authorities: a 12.5% Section 301 “forced labor” tariff on Chinese goods took effect July 24, 2026, explicitly positioned as more legally grounded than the invalidated emergency tariffs (Section 232 duties were unaffected by the ruling). Remarkably, this increase came despite a 1.8 mbd year-over-year contraction in refinery runs during the third quarter. Instead, the additional exports were supported by a 310 kbd decline in domestic diesel demand and inventory draws averaging 180 kbd over the quarter, pushing stocks below their five-year seasonal norms (Figure 6). With domestic diesel demand estimated at around 3.76 mbd this year, inventory coverage has already fallen sharply from roughly 32 days in April to about 24 days in October. China therefore has limited scope to sustain higher exports through further inventory draws. Additional barrels would need to come from a recovery in refinery runs and softer domestic demand following the Golden Week holidays, which would widen the exportable surplus. Based on our China diesel balance, the seasonal decline in domestic demand could allow exports to reach 600-700 kbd from October through year-end (Table 3). Achieving these volumes, however, would require a simultaneous recovery in refinery runs, supported by stronger crude imports and no rebuilding in domestic inventories. Taken together, China’s potential contribution could fill much of the remaining gap after European stock releases and additional Russian exports, potentially offsetting up to 90% of the current global diesel deficit by the end of the year. records.text: Euro Area Sovereign Risk: Now vs Then With European fiscal issues back in focus, investor questions about the possibility of renewed Euro area debt tensions have returned. So far, the bond market pressures have focused on France, with the OAT-Bund spread recently widening to decade highs (Exhibit 1). But we have also seen tentative signs of spillovers into other markets, including Italy. We thus explore the similarities and differences between the current situation and the 2011-15 European debt crisis. Similarities We see several similarities to the 2011-15 episode. First, fiscal imbalances are elevated in several Euro area economies (Exhibit 2). While public deficits are now notably narrower than in 2011-15 in some countries (Greece, Spain, Portugal), deficits are similar (France, Italy) or significantly higher in others (Belgium, Austria, Finland). Moreover, public spending needs have intensified further given pressures in health, pensions, climate and defence. The IMF, for example, estimates that these pressures will increase expenditures above current levels by about 4½pp of GDP by 2040 in Europe. records.text: US-China competition for metal tightens the ex-US market. China’s shortage n of scrap is increasing its need for refined copper, so far met by domestic inventory draws, just as the US continues to import and build inventory ahead of potential tariffs. With mine supply weaker than we previously expected, we now expect larger ex-US deficits of around 950kt in 2026 and 220kt in 2027 (vs. 640kt and 170kt previously). With US-China competition likely continuing to play out over the next year, combined with a higher positioning assumption, which partly reflects increased investor interest in hard assets, we raise our end-2026 copper forecast to $14,700/t from $13,735/t (vs. forwards at $14,437) and our 2027 average forecast to $15,400/t from $13,800/t (vs. forwards at $14,405). China increasingly needs refined copper to do the work previously done by n scrap. While copper cathode has always been the main material used in China to produce semi-fabricated products, scrap complemented it, driving on average 15% of copper semis production. However, a growing shortage of domestic scrap supply this year owing to more stringent scrap VAT invoicing has led semi-fabricators to increase their cathode demand, ultimately tightening China’s copper inventories. We set the sample size to ten years to capture a range of market regimes, and in particular beyond the recent tight spread regime. Two types of dependent variables: (1) 5-year CDS spreads for a subset of EM n sovereigns for which the data exhibit sufficient variation going back ten years or more, and, if not available, (2) option-adjusted spreads of Bloomberg country-specific sovereign USD bond indices.3 We regress weekly first differences on a constant and weekly changes of a set of n optimised variables and pre-imposed variables. We then back out spread levels by cumulating fitted contributions. We obtain the set of optimised variables for a given sovereign by picking the n combination of three variables from a pool of candidate market variables (see below) that maximises the R-squared of the regression, subject to pairwise correlation and variance inflation factor multicollinearity tests. The caveat is that we also include ‘pre-set’ variables. The resulting implications for credit are unlikely to be uniform across sectors, but instead flow through a relatively small number of policy transmission channels. Transmission channel #1: Fiscal policy, Deficits and Treasury supply For broad credit markets, the most important election-sensitive variable remains fiscal policy. The key question is not whether deficits remain elevated, but whether the election outcome increases or decreases the willingness of Congress to pursue additional spending initiatives, tax changes or fiscal packages. From a credit perspective, the impact is ultimately expressed through Treasury supply, rates and refinancing conditions. Credit spreads have remained resilient despite historically elevated Treasury issuance, but continued deficit expansion could keep upward pressure on long-end financing rates and increase competition for investor demand. Importantly, none of the potential election outcomes appear likely to fundamentally solve the deficit issue in our view. records.text: Smelters, by contrast, have continued to compete strongly for available secondary feed, with scrap use in smelting up 19% YoY YTD, as exceptionally tight concentrate supply and deeply negative spot treatment charges (TCs)2 increase the incentive to substitute towards scrap and scrap-derived anode. Smelters have also been relatively less affected by the VAT invoicing disruption, as they tend to source material through larger, more formalised suppliers. More recently, however, tightness in scrap-derived anode and other secondary feed has also begun to constrain the smelting chain, contributing to weaker refined copper output (Exhibit 6). In price terms, lower scrap availability in China adds $945/t to our end-2026 forecast and $2,985/t to our 2027 forecast, partly offset by higher scrap use by smelters, mainly outside China, where higher prices support collection (−$825/t and −$2,730/t). 2 Treatment charges are fees paid by miners to smelters for processing copper concentrate. Tight concentrate availability relative to smelting capacity has intensified competition for feedstock, pushing spot treatment charges below zero, meaning smelters effectively pay a premium to secure concentrate. records.text: M Idea 4 Importantly, despite the magnitude of the potential rebalancing, the longest-duration bonds have yet to become CTD in USZ6. Based on client conversations, we expect much of the associated flow to emerge only once that switch materializes. • Accordingly, we see little evidence that the technical selloff over the past two months has been materially driven by CTD-related rebalancing in US futures. Exhibit 3 supports this interpretation, showing changes in CFTC asset manager positioning over the past year. Although net asset manager longs declined through September and October, the reduction has been driven by increased gross shorts rather than liquidation of gross longs. • While lower net positioning reduces our estimate of potential rebalancing pressure, it does not suggest that asset managers have broadly reduced gross long exposure in anticipation of the CTD switch. The contract's convexity profile offers another explanation for the limited asset manager response. As the CTD shifts during a selloff, convexity declines under both risk methodologies and eventually turns negative (see Exhibit 4 ) • Once the switch occurs, further increases in yields can therefore begin to reduce the contract's duration. • This creates an incentive for investors to delay rebalancing until the CTD switch is more firmly established, as the ultimate duration adjustment may be smaller than the initial extension suggests. records.text: US Economics Weekly 16 October 2026 ab 27 US Economics Weekly UBS Research Data in the week ahead Monday, October 19 NAHB/Wells Fargo housing market index (Oct), 10:00 AM We expect the housing market index (HMI) was unchanged at 32 in October, following a 3-point decline in September. That said, we see risks as skewed to the downside as a consequence of the recent rise in mortgage rates, which weighs on affordability and likely kept demand contained. Based on current market pricing of ~3 additional hikes from both the Fed and ECB over the next 12 months and broadly stable spreads, we estimate that ICRs across US technology, healthcare and professional services will decline to 1.3x/1.8x/1.8x by end-2028 in the US (from 1.5x/1.9x/1.9x currently) (1) and to 1.2x/1.8x/1.7x in Europe ( from 1.4x/1.9x/1.9x currently) (2) . While these levels are low, they remain above the 1.0x threshold at which earnings no longer cover the interest on outstanding debt, implying that in aggregate, private credit can weather the higher interest rate environment for now. However, median ICRs above 1.0x can still be consistent with rising default rates in weaker parts of private credit. Given that technology loans account for ~25% of the private-credit universe in both the US and Europe, we estimate that a decline in the sector’s median ICR to 1.2x–1.3x by 2028, combined with pressure from elevated maturity walls, would be consistent with aggregate default rates rising by ~3% per year over the next two years. From current levels, this would result in the 12M default rate for US private credit rising to 7-8% by end-2027. If it assigns greater persistence to the shock or to its second-round effects, it could further strengthen the case for tightening. At 2.25%, the overnight rate sits at the bottom of the Bank’s estimated 2.25%-3.25% neutral range. If the BoC is placing greater weight on upside inflation risks, while viewing trade-related downside risks as more manageable, which was evident in the BoC Business Outlook Survey today, then the case for a modest preemptive adjustment becomes stronger. With headline inflation already above target, policymakers may judge the cost of waiting to be greater than the cost of moving the policy rate closer to the midpoint of neutral. However, core inflation continuing to run around 2% is a key risk to expectations for a hike, if the BoC decides they have room to assess the risks before adjusting policy. We continue to expect 0.25 pp hikes in October and January. The BoC's new forecasting model adds some uncertainty to their projections and how they view the risks from supply driven inflation. In the current political environment, Northern Virginia has had the most data center development in the U.S. The next four markets are Phoenix, AZ, Columbus, OH, Dallas, TX, and Atlanta, GA. While data center development and broader concerns around AI are likely to remain key policy issues, we believe the balance of power after the midterm elections will largely determine the pace of the data center buildout. If Democrats take both the House and the Senate in the upcoming midterm elections, we expect to see additional pressure to slow down data center growth given the significant pushback from communities, particularly around environmental impacts and affordability concerns. Under this scenario, we would expect modest underperformance from the Independent Power Producers (IPPs) such as VST, NRG, and TLN, as the growth of data centers becomes more measured. The Democratic party has emphasized its message that it would enforce more moratoriums and protect consumers with regulation and guardrails, promoting a strong anti-data center message at a time when AI concerns and community pushback are elevated. If Democrats only take control of the House and the Senate remains in Republican control, we expect the current pace of the data center buildout to continue. Forward earnings growth expectations have also increased, supported by positive revisions across several large sectors. Companies are therefore reporting into an improving earnings cycle, but not against a conventionally low bar. Key views in a nutshell 1. Estimates have risen into results. Where expectations have already improved, confirming consensus may not be enough to sustain outperformance. 2. Expected growth is strong, but highly dispersed. Consensus expects STOXX 600 revenue and EPS to grow 11% and 23%, respectively. Expected EPS growth varies materially across sectors, ranging from 135% in energy and 40% in materials to 24% in financials, 18% in industrials, 8% in technology and -5% in consumer discretionary. 3. The US imposes Section 232 national security tariffs on imported steel, aluminum and copper based on their full customs value and domestic metal content. A 50% tariff is applied to commodity steel, aluminum and copper articles made almost entirely of the metal. A 25% tariff is applied to general steel and aluminum derivative products, as well as other copper articles not covered by the 50% tier. We note that under current policy, steel and aluminum from the UK face a 25% tariff (or 15% for certain industrial/grid equipment) if composed of at least 95% UK-sourced metal. A Blue Wave scenario would likely drive some political pressure around tariffs as Democrats have argued they burden manufacturing, spike consumer/construction costs, and spark retaliatory friction with close allies. If the Democrats gain control of Congress, we expect more pressure on tariffs but limited ability to reverse them. Section 232 rests on authority Congress delegated under the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, so narrowing it requires new legislation. Overriding a veto requires two-thirds of both chambers. records.text: What to own when slowing growth meets narrow breadth Intensifying concerns about the cost and availability of funding have caused investors to reduce their equity market exposures and price a deceleration in the growth outlook. Rising energy prices and interest rates have weighed on the performance of many cyclical equities since early August. During the last two weeks, however, the potential implications of a sharply rising cost of capital on the AI build-out have weighed further on the market outlook for economic and earnings growth. Exacerbating these rotations, this week GS Prime Services noted a sharp reduction in hedge fund net leverage alongside a positioning pullback in AI-related stocks. Rates and credit markets have similarly reflected increasing pressure from funding costs and a downgrade to the outlook for growth. After climbing by more than 100 bp during the past six months, the 10-year Treasury yield has declined by more than 20 bp during the past two weeks. At the same time, USD high yield credit spreads widened by more than 20 bp, with pressure particularly concentrated in AI-related spreads alongside relative resilience in the defensive Energy and Utility sectors. Additionally, municipal waste incineration is to be gradually phased into the EU ETS starting in 2031. Inclusion of negative emissions Negative emissions are also to be integrated into the system, albeit in an indirect manner. "Negative emissions" refer to the active removal of CO₂ from the atmosphere. Between 2031 and 2040, the Commission plans to auction a total of 250 million additiona l emission allowances above the regular cap. This will increase the number of allowances for that decade by approximately 4.5%. For comparison, the overall ETS cap for 2026 stands at 1,185 million allowances. The revenues generated from these auctions will then be used to pay providers of permanent CO₂ removals. Under this mechanism, the volume of negative emissions acquired is intended to equal at least the emissions generated by the additional allowances. The guarantees are irrevocable and unconditional, but each guarantor is responsible for its own defined share rather than for the full EFSF obligation. If a borrower payment shortfall occurs, guarantors are initially called according to their contribution keys; if one fails to pay on time, EFSF can make additional calls on the others, up to the applicable over-guarantee limit. The over-guarantee therefore provides a buffer against an individual guarantor failing to pay, without making every member liable for the entire obligation. As detailed in EIB’s investor presentation, it is a fully capitalised multilateral development bank with €22.2bn of paid-in and €226.6bn of callable capital. France, Germany and Italy are its three largest shareholders, each accounting for around 18.8% of subscribed capital.

records.text: Agency MBS Weekly 16 October 2026 Citi Research 11 Fed custody holdings data and historical analogue suggest limited net selling risk… The Fed custody holdings data — the most timely indicator of foreign official positioning — shows $11-17bn selling of Treasuries per week over the past four weeks as the selloff intensified, while MBS holdings saw very limited changes (Figure 21). We note the data only captures security holdings of (primarily) foreign official institutions where the Federal Reserve Bank of New York acts as custodian; therefore, it only covers a subset of the foreign official holdings. T o assess the impact of selloff on private investors, we look to the late 2023 episode as an analogue. During the period, higher-for-longer sentiment — fueled by hotter-than-expected economic prints and sticky inflation — pushed 10-year yields to 5% in October. While this dampened foreign private demand, net purchases remained positive, and demand quickly recovered in the following months as yields began to rally (Figure 22). Arguably, inflation concerns were more pronounced during the 2023 episode. The resilience of net purchases against that backdrop suggests limited risk of net selling by foreign private investors in the current selloff, all else equal. Figure 21. An additional twist that will impact debt management decisions in coming quarters is the US statutory debt limit (debt ceiling) that is set to soon become a binding constraint. • The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) signed into law on July 4, 2025 raised the debt ceiling by $5tr to $41.1tr (see Exhibit 1 ). An increase in the debt limit does not authorize new spending. It simply increases the total amount of debt the US government can borrow to finance existing legal obligations. Once the debt limit becomes binding it will restrict the amount of debt authorized to be outstanding. So, Treasury will need to rely on a limited amount of extraordinary measures and draw down on its operating cash balance (TGA) to fund government spending. Shipments remained near 140 kbd, largely under intergovernmental agreements, including deliveries to Mongolia and other former Soviet Union countries. Additional volumes may have moved under exemptions, case-by-case approvals or alternative customs classifications, including flows to Turkey. Two factors likely explain why Russia has continued exporting diesel despite the restrictions. First, domestic storage capacity is limited, making it difficult to retain additional barrels that cannot be efficiently stored or distributed. Second, keeping diesel at home increases the fiscal burden through Russia’s fuel-damping mechanism. When refiners sell domestically rather than export at higher international netbacks, the government compensates them for part of the difference between domestic prices and export parity. As global diesel prices rise, these payments could increase, making export restrictions increasingly costly to maintain. Importantly, the TPI's eligibility criteria stipulate that support is available only for “jurisdictions experiencing a deterioration in financing conditions not warranted by country-specific fundamentals”. records.text: Despite September's stabilization, the long-awaited reversal of fiscal austerity has yet to materialize, as hinted by earlier credit and deposit data. Infrastructure investment – a more likely immediate fiscal beneficiary – stayed weak at -4.2%YoY Ytd vs. -4.0%YoY in Jan-Aug, but we expect the contraction to narrow as policy efforts come through. We maintain our GDP growth forecast at 4.6%YoY for both 26Q4E and 2026E, within the target range. This cyclical stabilization doesn't alleviate our concerns about 2027 and beyond (see: Approaching Inflection). Consumer confidence remains weak, with the urban household savings rate elevated at 39.2% in 26Q1-3 vs. 36.2% in pre-pandemic 19Q1-3. Property prices showed further signs of stabilization, while contractions in investment and sales both widened in September; the shift toward completed- home sales could weigh further on activities into 2027. Despite currently robust readings, early signs of peaking in the new economy may be emerging – chip output growth eased to 18.4%YoY in September, a six-month low, while industrial robot output slowed to 18.9%YoY, the weakest reading this year. We see 2027 as a more challenging year for China, likely prompting an inevitable policy pivot. The year- end Politburo meeting and CEWC could offer the earliest signals, and we expect more expansionary macro policy, including 20bps of rate cuts and a RMB2tn expansion in the general government deficit in 2027E. The Act became law on July 11 after passing 358-32 in the House and 85-5 in the Senate. It combines the House's Housing for the 21st Century Act and the Senate's ROAD to Housing Act of 2025. From January 7, 2027, it restricts institutional buying of single-family homes (defined as investors with 350 or more single-family homes). Existing portfolios are grandfathered, and build-to-rent and new construction are exempt. On supply, the Act directs the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to issue updated guidelines to help municipalities modernize zoning. It also streamlines National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) reviews, with exemptions for certain infill and affordable projects, and creates grants to convert vacant and commercial buildings into housing. It removes the permanent chassis requirement for manufactured homes, which should ease their placement and financing. On capital, it raises the cap on bank public welfare investments from 15% to 20%, freeing more private capital for Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC). Supply shocks The post-GFC low-rate environment was supported by the positive supply shock generated by shale oil. This led to a notable decline in long -term inflation expectations and the perception of inflation risks. It also enabled significantly more aggressive monetary policy easing, which culminated during Covid. Since then, however, the world economy has been subject to a succession of negative supply shocks: Covid, the Ukraine war, tariffs and the Iran war. While Covid may be an isolated one-off event, the other three shocks are the result of the current geopolitical environment. Moreover, there are arguably more potential flashpoints affecting critical supply chains in Asia or elsewhere. The consumption tax cut will not apply to alcoholic beverages and general dining out, and we calculate the weighting of food eligible for the tax cut is 21.5% for headline CPI, 18.4% for core CPI, and 20.0% for new core CPI. Mechanically applying the 7 percentage point tax cut depresses headline CPI by 1.5 pp, core CPI by 1.3 pp, and new core CPI by 1.4 pp for the year from April 2027 to March 2028 (Exhibit 7). Incorporating the consumption tax cut, our FY2027 inflation forecasts are +0.8% (+2.2% - 1.4%) for new core CPI and +1.1% (+2.4% - 1.3%) for core CPI. While the impact of the consumption tax cut will fade out of the year-on-year inflation rate in the second year of the tax cut from April 2028 to March 2029, mechanically CPI levels would rise again - by the same amount as the downward pressure from the tax cut - if the food consumption tax returns to 8% in April 2029. records.text: European Investment Grade Demand: Holding its ground Demand has held firm, though growth in credit holdings has slowed from previous years. The foundations of demand remain solid, and higher yields should provide a boost in 2027, even if some risks remain. Sterling demand is finding its footing as outflows slow and issuance picks up. Credit demand has held firm, though growth in holdings has slowed: European insurers, pension funds and investment funds continued to increase their credit holdings in the four quarters to Q2 26, but at a slower pace than previously. The moderation coincided with richer spread valuations and lower yields in the first half of the year, while allocations to credit are already near the top end of recent ranges. Higher yields help brighten the outlook for 2027: Yields stabilising at elevated levels may support insurance demand for credit via AUM growth, while higher all-in yields should bolster investment fund demand across both fixed maturity and traditional credit products. This tailwind will be much more powerful if rates volatility subsides, allowing investors to put cash to work. Demand should remain solid, though there are some potential headwinds: Political risk has returned as a consideration in Europe, with recent French sovereign stress highlighting the potential for spillovers into credit. records.text: Global Equity Strategy 19 October 2026 ab 17 Global Equity Strategy UBS Research Oil at a fulcrum: demand destruction at higher prices The Energy sector has typically tracked medium- and long-term oil expectations embedded in the forward curve rather than moves in spot prices. But spot and forward oil recently diverged, with forward prices basically flat as front month rose from <$90 in Aug to >$105 in early Sep while forward prices rose as oil price pressures alleviated some. This could potentially reflect demand-destruction concerns, as well as future supply/demand dynamics. More notably, Energy equities have also rallied more than forward oil prices, suggesting more is being priced unlike the early summer when Energy equities lagged oil futures moves. Time to start reducing Energy exposures. Our US REVS framework showed Energy at the top across sectors heading into Sep as the regime was shifting (Themes inflecting). Energy has notably outperformed of late, and is up over 50% YTD. With the potential to see demand destruction on even higher oil prices, particularly with less refining capacity globally pushing up product prices, we see less attractive risk reward in the sector and would be paring exposure and reallocating elsewhere. After Energy outperformance of Cap Goods and Transports as oil has jumped, we like reallocating some of that Energy risk to the Industrials. 2027 Housing Outlook: (Un)Affordability Starts to Bite Residential investment dropped in the first quarter of the year on the back of particularly poor weather before rebounding partially in the second and third quarters: after declining 8% annualized in Q1, residential fixed investment increased 3% in Q2 and, we estimate, 3% in Q3. In this Analyst, we summarize our outlook for the housing market for the rest of this year and 2027. Testing New Lows for Turnover Housing activity has remained rangebound in recent years, capped on the upside by affordability headwinds and buffered on the downside by the longstanding housing shortage. In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity. The left panel of Exhibit 2 shows that mortgage rates initially rebounded in March of this year in response to the Iran War, higher oil prices, and the prospect of Fed hikes and surged again over the last two months in part because policy rate expectations were revised higher. Our strategists expect mortgage rates to fall meaningfully next year— reflecting our dovish forecast for the Fed—but nonetheless remain elevated at 6.4%. However, the right panel of Exhibit 2 shows that even if the decline in mortgage rates we expect is realized, affordability will remain at historically poor levels (as measured by our strategists’ housing affordability index). records.text: M Update Morgan Stanley Research 3 we also caution that a likely reduction in employment growth projections is on the cards. But forecasting another forecast is a very tricky task. What we can say with certainty is that unlike into last year, expectations around this Budget appear largely relaxed or constructive. That, of course, creates a higher bar for outperformance, which remains our slight concern into October 28th. Beyond October, next year’s Spending Review will then be a key focus. Given the scale of shocks that have buffeted the UK economy in recent years, we are less concerned about this event than most. A lot can change until then, and our key focus for now remains on whether the Budget in two weeks brings a planned reduction in the headline and primary deficit between FY2026/27 and FY2027/28. Medium-term fiscal arithmetic is a challenge in every DM country with an elevated stock of debt, higher effective interest rates and aging population (see here for our an in-depth note on UK fiscal challenges, and our pan-European fiscal Blue Paper). Tackling these challenges all at once is implausible – consolidating one step at a time, instead, appears more realistic and arguably imperative. The UK has done better than most of its peers on that front in the past two years. We are constructive and believe that more is on the way, given the high level of scrutiny from international investors, whose capital inflows the UK needs to fund itself.

Finding short-run value signals in a tight spread world EM sovereign credit spreads have been on a tightening path since mid-2022 (Exhibit 1), reflecting the remarkable resilience of the asset class, which we have regularly documented in our EM Sovereign Credit Monitor. As suggested by our current EM Sovereign Credit model, EM spread valuations have been stretched since mid-2024 (Exhibit 1). Higher energy prices have so far been primarily a headline inflation story, with the impact on core inflation largely concentrated in airfares. We think this is likely to change. The persistence of the oil shock, rising transportation costs suggest that energy-related inflation could become increasingly visible across core goods. We have been expecting the bulk of this pass-through to materialize in 1Q27, when firms typically have greater scope to reset prices. However, September's stronger-than-expected CPI report raises the possibility that the process is beginning earlier than we anticipated. The persistence of the oil shock is key Historically, oil price shocks have had a relatively modest impact on core inflation. Our dynamic models suggest that a 10% supply-driven increase in oil prices raises core CPI by just 3–5bp, with most of the impact concentrated in a handful of categories. These estimates are consistent with the historical experience, in which higher oil prices tend to affect headline inflation relatively quickly but generate limited spillovers into core. However, there is an important caveat to these estimates: the historical dynamics implicitly assume that oil prices begin to decline roughly two to three months after the initial shock. Canada Economics Weekly 16 October 2026 Citi Research 2 A significant amount of data next week will determine the outcome of the October 28 rate decision, and if data align with our expectations, we would continue to expect policy rates remaining unchanged at 2.25% this month. Most important will be September CPI data on Monday, which is likely to show headline inflation rising a bit above the target range to 3.2% due to higher gas prices. At the September rate decision, Governor Macklem had sounded particularly sensitive to too-high headline inflation, implying hawkish implications of above-3% headline CPI. But details in the summary of deliberations from the September decision make us think the decision to raise rates would still be tied to seeing evidence that higher energy prices are feeding through to other prices: With the economy still in excess supply and the labour market soft, weaker growth from the trade conflict could keep inflationary pressures contained. However, if higher energy prices did spill over into other components of the CPI, members agreed that it could require a monetary policy response to prevent broad-based inflation from setting in. We think officials will tolerate headline CPI slightly above 3% for a period as long as core inflation measures remain subdued. In our base case, various core inflation measures all remain around 2% in next week’s data. Core measures broadly climbing towards or above 2.2-2.3% may be strong enough for a hike in October.

OAT-Bund spreads: directionality, cheapness, risks ahead Among field trip participants, there was broad agreement on the fact that part of the widening in OAT-Bund spreads had to do with the rise in the overall level of EUR rates, given the higher financing costs weighed on interest expenses and thereby made the budgetary equation more complicated. Interest expenditure is also a metric that rating agencies focus on but those could still argue that France’s elevated weighted average maturity of debt means that higher yields would have to persist for longer to have a meaningful impact on total interest burden. OAT-Bund spreads were seen to incorporate some cheapness related to recent technical flows (eg. stop losses on long ASW positions), but clients noted that the length of the budgetary process, the positioning for increased supply in Q1 and election uncertainty could limit appetite to fade this cheapness. ECB action in case of renewed widening was seen by clients to be focused on verbal intervention, with slowing of QT as next step but considered at much wider levels and under contagion to other EGBs. Our baseline of a 100-150bp range for 10y OAT-Bunds in the next few months was seen as optimistic by clients, although many thought peak uncertainty and pressure would be later in 1Q27.

The Government’s signalling in recent n weeks points to a cautious approach to the Autumn budget, with an aim to rebuild headroom and fund temporary cost of living relief through a series of smaller, targeted tax measures. Chancellor Healey has placed a clear emphasis on fiscal restraint, and many of the larger, more ambitious spending projects and flagship policies are expected either after a 2027 spending review or for a policy platform into the next general election. Spending pressures into these future events still appear meaningful, with higher defence spending requirements a key issue, alongside welfare spending projects (particularly on social care). But it is far from clear that the balance of recently unveiled policy initiatives are a net negative for Sterling. EU reintegration would stand to be a significant positive for the currency through a boost to growth, albeit a very slow-moving process. And the Government’s revealed preference to tackle the politically sensitive triple lock on pensions is the type of step that should help shore up their fiscal credibility. Perhaps most importantly, these signs of spending restraint and newfound political stability come at a time when fiscal premia are rising in other major markets (see EUR bullet). records.text: 32 Tarek HamidAC (1-212) 834-5468 tarek.x.hamid@jpmorgan.com North America Credit Research 16 October 2026 J P M O R G A N HG & HY Automotive The 2026 U.S. midterm elections are unlikely to reset the policy backdrop for High Grade and High Yield Automotive credits immediately. The Automotive ecosystem will nonetheless remain prominent in debates over trade policies, domestic manufacturing, and consumer affordability. USMCA remains unresolved, while other issues may depend more on executive action or the 2028 election cycle than the composition of the next Congress. We examine these policy channels below. USMCA remains the principal, unresolved auto policy issue. The United States declined to extend the agreement at its July 2026 joint review, but the existing USMCA remains in force while negotiations continue. We expect any revised agreement will define the tariff and rules-of-origin framework governing North American auto production through the early 2030s. The U.S. midterm election results would not itself change the agreement or the existing Section 232 tariffs on imported vehicles and parts. It could, however, affect congressional oversight of the negotiations and the path for any changes that require U.S. legislation. The key aspects of a new USMCA or bilateral trade agreements, in our view, are whether a revised framework changes rules of origin, U.S. and regional content requirements, or tariff treatment for vehicles and parts moving across North American borders.
