Second-hand housing prices improved: New home sales by floor space fell 16.9% y/y in Q3, compared with a 12.7% y/y decrease in Q2. However, on the pricing front, second-hand housing prices in tier-1 cities edged up 0.2% m/m in September, up from the 0.1% m/m increase in August. Meanwhile, the decline in tier-2 cities narrowed to 0.2% m/m in September from a 0.3% m/m drop in August, while the decline in second-hand housing prices in tier-3 cities remained steady at 0.3% m/m . China's new property policies signal that policymakers are actively working to stabilise the sector rather than just leaving it to market forces. Nonetheless, we expect the impact on property sales and investment to remain mild. As such, we still expect a little more downturn in the property sector before a recovery begins (see China: Q4 mini stimulus package to provide mild b oost,dated 29 September) . records.text: Global FX Strategy 15 October 2026 Citi Research 2 We also note Fed pricing has now moved to only 4bps for October and cumulative 26bps for December. Omitting country-specific duration from our USD spread model Unlike with the 5-year CDS model, which is tenor-specific, the USD spread regression model is based on spread indices that aggregate bonds across tenors. A way to adjust for the effect of different sovereign spread index duration is simply to control for country-specific duration. We initially estimated the USD spread model by controlling for duration (as a pre-set variable), but this approach led to discrete jumps in fair values around the time sovereigns issued large amounts of new bonds (for example, Mexico and Kuwait in 2025), which were not reflected in the realised spread data. This reinforces our view that large amounts of EM bond supply have not catalysed spread widening in recent years, and issuance has been well absorbed across EM IG and HY. Further, controlling for country-specific duration does not lead to materially higher explanatory power, so we omit this variable altogether in the USD spread model. Although terms-of-trade exposures typically provide a useful signal of relative FX performance following a given commodity-price shock, there are some exceptions. CHF is one example, as Switzerland’s large gold imports and exports—re flecting its role as a refining hub— results in a less reliable relationship between CHF and the terms-of-trade signal from a gold price shock. In such cases, a simple historical beta to commodity prices may provide a more useful gauge of FX sensitivity. Trading Terms of Trade We have previously shown how our commodity terms of trade indices can benefit systematic trading strategies, particularly when commodity-price volatility is elevated. However, despite the fact that shifts in our GSTOT indices have been clearly correlated with relative returns over the course of this year’s energy shock, the strength of the relationship on the surface has disappointed relative to 2022. In other words, a simple strategy that goes long the three currencies with the largest one-week improvements in GSTOT and short the three with the largest deteriorations—rebalanced weekly—has generated weaker returns (Exhibit 8). We continue to attribute this weaker performance to commodity price volatility relative to rates and equity market volatility. records.text: US Economics Weekly 16 October 2026 Citi Research 2 In our view, the most important development this week was not the data itself but rather the market reaction to it. Stronger-than-expected core inflation for September led us to pencil in one additional 25bp rate hike in December. But after briefly moving higher, Treasury yields fell as equity prices declined, reflecting concerns about whether revenue can grow fast enough to justify lofty valuations. For the last few months, markets were treating the economy as if it would be impervious to higher interest rates. As markets revised-up expectations for rate hikes, that meant longer-term Treasury yields moved higher as well. But this week, the first signs are emerging that markets are falling into a more familiar pattern where higher interest rates today mean slower growth ahead, leading to declining equity prices and lower longer-term yields. Ultimately, this dynamic can limit central bank appetite for rate hikes. If credit spreads widen and equity prices fall further, officials would conclude that financial conditions have already meaningfully tightened, making them reluctant to deliver further policy rate increases. However, tighter tax administration may also have contributed. Since 2H25, listed companies’ income tax expenses have grown faster than their pre-tax profits, suggesting a rising effective tax burden. More listed companies have also reported higher taxes and surcharges, although these increases have coincided with stronger operating revenue. Meanwhile, amid China’s anti-tax-evasion campaign, at least 80 listed companies were reportedly required to pay back corporate income tax and late-payment charges in 1H26, compared with 89 cases in full-year 2025. To further tighten the market, holdings in the so-called Market Stability Reserve have since been capped at a maximum of 400 million allowances, while excess (unused) permits permanently expire. Under the current reduction pathway, the volume of newly issued allowances would mathematically fall to zero by 2039/2040. Proposed adjustments for greater industrial flexibility The Commission’s reform proposal now aims to lower the linear annual reduction factor from the currently projected 4.4% to 3.7% starting in 2031. From 2036 onwards, the factor is then set to stand at 1.7%. This slows down the annual decline in the volume of allowances and is intended to give indu stry more time and flexibility to decarbonise. Additionally, the Market Stability Reserve is to be adjusted to further cushion extreme price spikes. One proposal under discussion is to halt the automatic cancellation of unused allowances held in the reserv e (which currently applies to any volume exceeding 400 million). Instead of being cancelled, these allowances would be released back to emitters if market prices rise sharply. For industrial sectors subject to the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), the allocation of free allowances is to be extended by four years, meaning the complete phase -out will not be finalised until 2038. The South African Reserve Bank (SARB) has been explicit in characterising the oil shock as persistent rather than temporary, while focusing increasingly on the risk that externally generated price pressures spill over into domestic inflation and expectations. Its hawkish bias could become materially more entrenched if the 21 October CPI report provides evidence that price pressures are broadening beyond energy. MKT MediaStats Hawkish/Dovish readings for the SARB have become progressively more hawkish in recent months, a shift increasingly reflected in rate expectations (Figure 3). Real money positioning in the ZAR remains neutral – see here – while maintaining an adequate real rate buffer will be important in underpinning currency stability (Figure 4). With near-term rate hikes already priced, potential value may instead lie further out the curve should heightened inflation risks push the SARB’s hawkish bias up another notch. records.text: Housing activity has remained rangebound in recent years, capped on the upside n by affordability headwinds and buffered on the downside by the longstanding housing shortage. In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability—reignited by the recent rebound in mortgage rates—to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity. Sustained higher mortgage rates will continue to have their most pronounced n impact on housing turnover, and the recent run-up in rates is likely to push existing home sales lower in the coming months. More than 95% of mortgage borrowers have interest rates below current market rates, and 65% have rates 2pp below market rates, strongly disincentivizing them from moving. As a result, we expect existing home sales to total just 3.9mn in 2027, 26% below 2019 levels (albeit only modestly below our forecast of 4.0mn for 2026, as our strategists expect 30-year fixed mortgage rates to fall to 6.4% by the end of next year on account of our dovish forecast for the Fed). The housing shortage has kept single-family homebuilding extremely resistant to n higher interest rates: single-family starts have declined by 3% so far this year compared to last year but have averaged 3% above 2019 levels despite 3½pp higher mortgage rates today. Some context on Fed pricing Estimates of neutral are time-varying, have wide confidence intervals and can be substantially revised over time. That being said, we have long argued that the drivers behind the post-GFC decline in equilibrium rates had reversed. Our updated debt-sustainability model assumes that fiscal policy, growth, inflation, and sovereign yields evolve in line with historical regularities, and estimates the effect of the projected fiscal trajectory on public debt. For Spain, we assume that the primary balance converges to 0.2% of GDP and real growth to 1.2% by 2032, consistent with past policy and our estimate of potential growth. We find that Spain remains an exception, with the debt-to-GDP ratio declining to 95% by 2030 even if yields stabilise at their highest level in a decade. records.text: line roughly two to three months after the initial shock. In other words, these models are largely capturing the consequences of a temporary increase in energy prices. That assumption looks increasingly inappropriate given the persistence of the current shock. A complementary approach is to use input-output models, which trace the role of energy costs through the production and distribution chains of different goods and services. Unlike historical dynamic models, this framework allows us to consider the consequences of a permanent increase in oil prices. The results are substantially different. While our dynamic models suggest that a 10% oil price increase raises core CPI by just 3–5bp, our input-output estimates imply a cumulative increase in the core CPI price level of roughly 20bp if the oil shock is permanent. Input-output models provide limited information about the timing of price adjustments, and firms may absorb some of the additional costs through lower margins rather than passing them on to consumers. However, the comparison illustrates an important point: the longer energy prices remain elevated, the greater the risk that historical models understate the eventual inflationary impact.

The aftereffects of a hot European summer have hampered the recovery of French nuclear availability into the shoulder season, driven by a combination of low river levels and low flow rates leading to cooling-related outages at various reactors. In late September, EDF announced that output at its Civaux power plant could be temporarily reduced from 1 October due to low flow rates of the Vienne River, and at the start of this month, the Civaux 1 and Civaux 2 reactors suffered short-lived forced outages of around 1GW due to “environmental issues”. The return of Chooz 1 and Chooz 2 – which have been out due to river cooling issues since July – have also been constantly delayed, with the plants now expected to return only on 30 October. The direction of travel is toward a higher resting inflation rate, with supply shocks playing an increasing role in driving elevated inflation outcomes. Sticky inflation from multiple sources We have accounted for this in two ways in our inflation and monetary policy outlook. First, following the failure of the MOU to hold, we shifted to a permanent oil risk-premium baseline where we penciled in stronger second-round effects of higher energy prices into core inflation (see here). Our analysis indicates that second-round effects from higher energy prices could show through in airline fares, apparel, new and used vehicles, and motor vehicle equipment and supplies, among other items (see here and here). Airline fares are up substantially, rising 23% y/y, and the September CPI report included strong readings in the remaining categories. Is this a sign of newly emergent second-round effects on good prices that will offset diminishing price pressures from tariffs? It is hard to say for sure, but an important driver in our outlook for disinflation is the end of tariff pass- through. records.text: Term premium has risen by 150-200bp across the G4 since 2021. We introduce a n new modeling framework to understand better what drives term premium and what levels today’s macro environment implies. We benchmark term premium against the level of inflation, macro and policy rate n uncertainty, the cyclical position, central bank bond holdings, and fiscal risks. This exercise explains the recent rise across most markets well, with bond supply via elevated deficits and smaller central bank balance sheets responsible for about half of the explained increase over the last half decade. Macro uncertainty and inflation explain most of the rest. The AI capex cycle brings upside risk to term premium by increasing debt supply n to finance the buildout and by potentially raising the sensitivity of yields to the overall debt supply. At the same time, the succession of supply shocks since the pandemic has complicated the growth/inflation tradeoff for central banks, leading to an erosion of the hedge value of bonds in a balanced portfolio, which is consistent with higher term premium. Our primary approach focuses on domestic drivers, but the recent selloff has n been common across the G10. records.text: How do we think about this potential technology advancement by CXMT? While we acknowledge that CXMT’s technological progress could negatively affect market sentiment, we believe it is still too early to assess the impact on the fundamentals of the leading DRAM players such as SEC and Hynix. A clearer assessment of this new technology would require considerably more information than what has been disclosed so far, including CXMT’s current development stage (e.g., is it a R&D sample or a customer sample?), cost competitiveness (compared to already existing products in the market), expected yield rate, customer qualification timeline, and commercialization timeline. Based on the articles, CXMT would currently appear to be at the product design stage and is targeting the sampling stage by the end of 2026. While the technology itself could potentially be an achievement if the company is successful in meeting the target timeline, we still believe the company likely has significant ground to cover—particularly because customer qualification and mass production would present an entirely different levels of difficulty to achieve. Furthermore, given the advanced roadmaps of SEC and Hynix, the core debate surrounding 4F² is governed not by technical feasibility in the lab, but by whether the architecture can actually deliver manufacturing productivity and economic return. Uncertainty in decarbonisation investments The reaction of the European business community is likely to be sceptical, albeit for different reasons. For companies focused on the EU internal market with limited competition from outside the EU (e.g., the power sector within the EU ETS), both reform pr oposals offer some relief, but they also raise fundamental questions. Investments in decarbonisation are economically viable primarily when CO₂ prices are high, or more precisely, when CO₂ abatement costs are below the CO₂ price. However, a slower reductio n pathway for emission allowances has – ceteris paribus – a dampening effect on prices. The reform proposals could undermine businesses' confidence in the ability of policymakers to withstand pressure from industry and the public as CO₂ prices rise. We think officials will tolerate headline CPI slightly above 3%YoY in September due to higher gas prices, but will keep rates unchanged as long as various core inflation measures remain around 2% (our base case). Conclusion The proposed easing of the linear reduction factor in the first half of the 2030s would dampen the upward pressure on carbon allowance prices compared to the current regime. Furthermore, the parliamentary report’s proposed intervention threshold for price fluctuations over 25% could reduce allowance price volatility. While both the Commission's draft and the Parliament's proposal offer some meaningful relief to industry, the emissions path will remain very ambitious . The Parliament’s draft goes further by pushing back the implementation of the strictest requirements by a few years, while retaining them in principle. As a result, the challenges facing businesses are not eliminated, but merely deferred. In terms of analogous electoral setups, the 2006 election ended with a Republican president and Democratic control of Congress with the High Grade market 7bp tighter and High Yield market +4% in the following three months. Conversely, the 2018 election ended with a Republican president, Republican Senate and Democratic House. The High Grade market was 9bp wider and High Yield returned +1.8% in the subsequent three months. This time will probably be similar, in our view, and we suspect the Fed, inflation, deficits, rates and corporate earnings will probably have a bigger impact on credit markets than the election. See inside for more historical context and thoughts around transmission mechanisms from our strategy teams. Data centers and AI touch everything. We could write an entire note about the potential impact of different regulatory regimes on the AI and data center buildout. In the heat of the election it appears one thing that unites Democrats and Republicans is a negative disposition towards data centers and desire to create an AI regulatory framework. The nuances of how that plays out have enormous implications across the economy from Technology to Real Estate, Power and Energy. Based on our latest analysis, the average BDC technology loan remains marked near 93-94c in aggregate (vs. 88-89c in the broadly syndicated loan market) as of the latest Q2’26 filings, with a distressed ratio of ~5% versus ~20% in BSL technology. However, aggregate marks hide meaningful dispersion across vintages. Technology loans from the weaker 2021 vintage are marked closer to ~85c on average, compared with ~92c for 2022 and ~95c across most subsequent vintages, consistent with lower non-accrual rates in these cohorts. This suggests that private lenders are recognizing stress selectively, even if aggregate marks appear relatively resilient. We see a similar pattern among technology borrowers that we classify as having mid or high exposure to AI disruption risk in our bottom-up framework : there has not been broad-based deterioration across the basket as a whole, but a smaller tail of troubled borrowers 1. In the US, we estimate that Technology, Business Services and Healthcare represent 23%, 33%, and 14% of the private credit universe. 2. OAT-Bund spreads: directionality, cheapness, risks ahead Among field trip participants, there was broad agreement on the fact that part of the widening in OAT-Bund spreads had to do with the rise in the overall level of EUR rates, given the higher financing costs weighed on interest expenses and thereby made the budgetary equation more complicated. Interest expenditure is also a metric that rating agencies focus on but those could still argue that France’s elevated weighted average maturity of debt means that higher yields would have to persist for longer to have a meaningful impact on total interest burden. OAT-Bund spreads were seen to incorporate some cheapness related to recent technical flows (eg. stop losses on long ASW positions), but clients noted that the length of the budgetary process, the positioning for increased supply in Q1 and election uncertainty could limit appetite to fade this cheapness. ECB action in case of renewed widening was seen by clients to be focused on verbal intervention, with slowing of QT (Quantitative Tightening) as next step but considered at much wider levels and under contagion to other EGBs. Our baseline of a 100-150bp range for 10y OAT-Bunds in the next few months was seen as optimistic by clients, although many thought peak uncertainty and pressure would be later in 1Q27.

Figure 5 shows how DOV varies with OTR yield (across the shifted yield sce- narios) for USZ6, and Figure 6 shows the same for WNZ6. Turning to WNZ6, the peak in DOV according to our model is ~20bp above the current 30Y OTR yield. Stronger fiscal revenue partly supported by tighter tax administration Admittedly, stronger fiscal revenue partly reflects improving industrial profits, supported by a recovery in PPI inflation and the tech-sector boom. However, tighter tax administration may also have contributed. Since 2H25, listed companies’ income tax expenses have grown faster than their pre-tax profits, suggesting a rising effective tax burden. Meanwhile, amid China’s anti-tax-evasion campaign, at least 80 listed companies were reportedly required to pay back corporate income tax and late-payment charges in 1H26, compared with 89 cases in full-year 2025. records.text: Japan Rates Weekly 16 October 2026 Citi Research 3 JGBs forming range The JGB market is firm, having smoothly digested recent auctions. The 10y yield has fallen below 3% and there appears to be a change in the uptrend in interest rates seen in July-September. Supply/demand is favorable compared to overseas markets, and the steep curve prices in an ample risk premium. We think for interest rates to start to rise again would require increased upward momentum by interest rates overseas or a strengthening in fiscal concerns. In overseas markets, US interest rates have similarly declined from recent peaks. The US September CPI exceeded market forecasts, and at one point there were heightened expectations for an October rate hike. Our US Economist Team has now changed to an outlook for a Fed rate hike in December. Interest rates subsequently turned downward on market concern about the AI boom. Now we can only wait to see if risk-off sentiment is merely temporary. Uncertainty remains ahead of the midterm elections, and that the budget deficit is expected to remain large thereafter remains a factor weighing on the market. Other than position adjustment due to technical factors, we think there is a lack of catalysts to drive a decline in interest rates. In Europe, France remains the focus: the spread with Bunds remains wide, and given the long process toward the next election, this is unlikely to subside soon. Greater central government support is therefore increasingly necessary to ease local fiscal constraints and prevent a rising effective tax burden from offsetting spending support. While we have yet to see additional central government bond issuance aimed at supporting the broader economy, the release of RMB550bn in unused local government bond quotas on Oct 9 is a welcome development. Similar to the RMB500bn allocation in last Oct, this should provide additional funding to local governments, ease fiscal and debt pressures, and support investment, helping lay the groundwork for reflation. The key question is how quickly these quotas translate into bond issuance and actual spending. Ultimately, we believe the policy objective should extend beyond stabilizing near-term activity to turning expectations around. Overall, the data are calling for another hike in October, but it is a very close call. With the market pricing only 4bp for October, delivering a hike would mean surprising the market just before the midterm elections. On the other hand, it would be the perfect way for Warsh to gain credibility at the helm of the Fed. We stick to our call for 25bp hikes in October and December. records.text: of fiscal reform over many years, the French government should request an Outright Monetary Transactions (OMT) programme, the facility established during the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis in 2012 under Mario Draghi's leadership. Under an OMT programme, a country must adhere to “ strict and effective conditionality attached to an appropriate European Financial Stability Facility/European Stability Mechanism (EFSF/ESM) programme”. Such a programme can take the form of either a full EFSF/ESM macroeconomic adjustment programme or a precautionary programme (Enhanced Conditions Credit Line) provided it includes the possibility of EFSF/ESM primary market purchases. However, pursuing such a programme would likely entail significant political costs, which is one reason why the OMT facility has never been activated. We believe that requesting an OMT programme would be out of the question for the French government. Could the ECB end QT to help France? Former ECB official Lorenzo Bini Smaghi recently argued that, "in the current stress", the ECB should halt quantitative tightening (QT), in other words, the practice of allowing government bonds previously purchased under its QE programmes (APP and PEPP) to roll off its balance sheet as they mature. According to Bini Smaghi, "[t]his policy means that a larger share of the net supply of government bonds has to be absorbed by private investors, at a time when long-term rates are already under upward pressure." Viewed this way, the abruptness of the shift from growth opti- mism to fears about fiscal sustainability is striking. But the (r - g) calculation for debt stabilisation may also have become somewhat unbalanced: long-tem interest rates (r) may have increased more quickly than assessments of the longer-term growth trend (g) and the neutral policy rate. A correction by either part would reduce the fiscal challenge. Has the (r - g) calculation gone too far? A Clear Election Outcome Could Unlock Further Bonos Re-Rating Since the mid-1990s, general elections have typically been followed by fiscal tightening, except during crisis periods—the GFC and sovereign debt crisis—and in 2018. The snap election also has the potential advantage of decoupling Spain’s political uncertainty from the broader European electoral cycle. If the election on 29 November delivers a clear majority and a government with the political capacity to approve a budget, we think Spanish sovereign debt could re-rate. Opinion polls point to a solid lead for the centre-right Partido Popular (PP) over the incumbent centre-left PSOE, significantly wider than at the 2023 election. The polls are also consistent with a PP–Vox coalition securing a comfortable parliamentary majority and delivering a change in government (Exhibit 6). Although a policy agenda has yet to be fully specified, a new coalition would likely act along three dimensions: accelerating debt reduction through further fiscal consolidation; removing sector-specific levies, including the bank tax; and facilitating private residential investment while pursuing tighter immigration policy. records.text: ab 16 October 2026 Global Research European Rates Strategy EU credit: how much does France really matter? Key takeaways  France alone is unlikely to trigger an EU downgrade. Fitch’s support test is centred on AAA-rated members, while Moody’s and S&P benefit from diversification across member states.  Member-state support remains the key credit anchor. Rating pressure would arise if deterioration among highly rated members reduced their capacity to support EU debt service, or if their willingness to do so weakened.  Political risk looks more relevant longer term. Resistance to further fiscal integration may threaten the future size and permanence of the EU bonds before it threatens the creditworthiness of the existing stock. Following our recent work on EU bonds, client questions have increasingly shifted from supply and spreads to the foundations of the credit itself: what happens if a member state cannot pay, and would another downgrade of France pull down the EU rating? The question is particularly timely ahead of Moody’s scheduled review of France on 23 October. Moody’s is currently lagging S&P and Fitch, rating France Aa3/ Negative, while both S&P and Fitch have already moved France into the single-A category at A+/Stable. Our analysis suggests that even a further French downgrade would not mechanically translate into an EU downgrade. EM sovereign credit spreads have been on a tightening path since mid-2022, n which has led to stretched fundamental valuations and asymmetric return prospects across the board. Against that backdrop, episodes of volatility, such as the current bout led by rates, can open up tactical relative value opportunities that longer-term fair values might fail to capture. In this Global Markets Analyst, we introduce an alternative, higher-frequency model of EM sovereign credit spreads, which aims to estimate cyclical fair values using only global market variables and to identify short-run value signals. We regress EM 5-year CDS and USD bond spreads on combinations of global n market variables that maximise the R-squared of the regression. We find that this ‘global’ model performs well in explaining EM sovereign spread changes, with elevated R-squared coefficients for a large share of sovereigns. Our analysis points to a number of high-frequency undervaluation signals in EM n 5-year CDS spreads, which we largely attribute to realised dynamics not fully reflecting the ‘EM-friendly’ improvement in risk factors. In turn, we find pockets of value in USD bond spreads, particularly among oil-exporting sovereigns. At the country level, we see room for the CDS of Colombia, South Africa, Chile n and Saudi Arabia to tighten, in line with their global betas, recent underperformance and support from higher-for-longer oil prices. Conclusions Taken together, the fundamental fiscal challenges look harder now than in 2011-15. In most countries, the starting level of debt is higher, structural spending pressures are more pronounced, bond yields are rising quickly and political fragmentation complicates the required fiscal adjustment. These challenges are particularly pronounced in France. That said, the threat of disorderly market escalation and real economy contagion looks lower. Nominal growth is notably stronger, external imbalances are lower, banks are in much better shape and the EMU institutional framework has been clarified. The risk of a disorderly bond market crisis (with multiple market equilibria) has therefore been notably reduced. But the issue of how to deal with fundamental sovereign risk in the monetary union remains unresolved without a fiscal union and ultimately requires credible fiscal consolidation. Under a Republican Congress, we expect current policy to continue. Under a divided government, we expect more scrutiny of consumer costs, but limited ability to reverse executive tariffs. For packaging, the net effect is a change in mix rather than a loss of volume. Fewer cross-border small parcels are partly offset by more domestic fulfillment. Lumber and pulp tariffs are likely to remain in place, so we don’t expect any material movement here. US tariffs on Canadian softwood lumber total ~45%. A separate 50% Section 338 tariff, with no USMCA exemption, applies to a broad range of Canadian wood, pulp and paper products. These include dissolving pulp, kraft linerboard, corrugated boxes, tissue, printing and writing papers and coated paperboard. Canada responded with counter-tariffs of up to 50% on US pulp, paper and packaging. Under a Republican Congress, we expect the tariffs to stay in place. Under a divided government, we expect more pressure for a settlement, though Section 338 authority stays with the President, subject to court challenges. Softwood lumber would likely stay on its own track through Commerce's annual duty reviews. As a result, the ECB may find it difficult to justify ending QT specifically to support France rather than relying on these instruments. Will the ECB hike the MRR? Press reports from late June suggested that the ECB is considering raising the minimum reserve requirement (MRR) from 1% to 2%, with a decision potentially due in the autumn. The MRR applies to selected bank liabilities, primarily customer deposits and debt securities with maturities of up to two years. We estimate that an increase to 2% would reduce excess liquidity (EL) by around €170bn and lower the ECB's annual interest payments to banks by up to €4.3bn (assuming a deposit rate at 2.5%). Savings could be smaller if the ECB combines a higher MRR with a tiering system. Eurosystem excess liquidity currently stands at €2.1tn, down from a peak of €4.7tn. As quantitative tightening (QT) continues, liquidity will eventually become scarce. Our previous research suggests this will occur around mid-2028, when EL falls to about €1.25tn. We think a higher MRR would bring this point forward by several months, potentially to early 2028. Morgan Securities LLC Global Markets Strategy U.S. Fixed Income Markets Weekly 16 October 2026 JPMORGAN As we are just over two weeks out from the midterm elections, one of the questions we have been receiving is how much election premium is priced into swaptions markets . To address this question, we examine the changes in 1M expiry swaption implied volatility in the first week of October (when the midterms rolled into the expiry window) in relation to 2-week expiry swaption implieds (for which the midterms remain outside the option win- dow). This allows us to infer the midterm premium currently priced into swaptions. We start by estimating the beta between 1M expiry implied vols and 2W expiry implied vols, which was 0.8 at the beginning of October for 10-year tails. This beta, taken together with the daily change in 2Wx10Y implied volatility, gives an expected change in 1Mx10Y implied volatility. We then compare the actual day-over-day changes with this expected change. As can be seen in Figure 12, this beta has been positive in every sector, around 0.2 bp/day. IG fundamentals can absorb higher rates: IG issuers start with low leverage and improving earnings. With most debt fixed- coupon and nearly two-thirds of EUR IG bonds maturing in 2030 or beyond, higher yields will feed through to funding costs only gradually. Even if earnings stall, ICRs would decline only gradually, and stronger EBITDA growth could improve them. Lower-rated HY is more exposed: The broader HY market shows similarly encouraging trends, with low aggregate leverage and ICRs above historical averages. Lower-rated issuers, however, are more exposed, as B- and CCC names have relatively more front-loaded maturities, alongside higher leverage and weaker ICRs than their ratings imply. We continue to expect further decompression across HY ratings, with single-Bs most vulnerable to higher-for-longer rates. Morgan Securities LLC Global Markets Strategy U.S. Fixed Income Markets Weekly 16 October 2026 JPMORGAN Cleaning up ABS We provide an update on the execution of the optional clean-up calls in amortizing sectors such as auto loan ABS and CLN pools, equipment ABS and unsecured consumer market- place lending (MPL) ABS. In ABS, the cleanup call is generally undertaken to handle the administrative costs and challenges that come with managing a very small remaining bal- ance of loans. Seasoned collateral from called pools is factored down enough to be sprinkled into new pools for refi. Most sponsors exercise the options consistently even during rate/ market volatility and through economic cycles. This is reflected in the primary and second- ary market, with ABS usually pricing to call as the default. In contrast in RMBS and CMBS, the use of call options and their execution is an economic decision for the seller/servicer that’s tied much closer to prevailing interest rates, collateral value and refinancing market conditions. Meanwhile, data next week should confirm inflation is, still, far from being well-behaved. Long story short, the trade-off for monetary policy shows some signs of shifting, which reinforces the need for a hike in November. Indeed, resilient GDP data this week, supported by AI spending, strengthens the case for a November hike. The economy continues to be resilient and is faring better than expected in the midst of rising energy prices and tighter financial conditions. And services have been mainly driving the resilience of the economy for most of the year. And data next week is unlikely to derail a hike in November, barring significant downside surprises. Inflation is likely to print way above the BoE forecasts (see below for the preview of the data). More importantly, services inflation is expected to pick up. The big upside surprise in headline inflation vs BoE’s forecast and the firming up of underlying services inflation could further strengthen the case for a hike in November. What I try to do in thinking about what’s going on, I try to look out the window as clearly as I can." FRB of New York President Williams noted that he sees one additional rate hike in 2026 as appropriate if the outlook evolves broadly in line with his expectations. "If the outlook kind of plays out broadly consistent with my expectations, I haven't changed my view that it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike. Attention now turns to monetary policy and the September inflation release. The South Africa PriceStats index indicates renewed acceleration in prices, with levels exceeding 2022, driven largely by the renewed rise in crude oil and petroleum costs (Figure 1). In other words, the relationship is non-linear: the higher the prevailing inflation rate, the greater the pass-through to CPI from an oil price shock. records.text: longstanding—but moderating, as discussed below— nationwide housing shortage, as households are often simply switching between housing units and no housing units are created or destroyed. Still, turnover has meaningful implications for GDP , as fewer existing home sales lower residential fixed investment via brokers’ commissions (which account for roughly 15% of RFI). Less Support From the Housing Shortage for Single-family Homebuilding The longstanding housing shortage has kept single-family homebuilding extremely resistant to higher interest rates: single-family starts have declined by 3% so far this year compared to last year but have averaged 3% above 2019 levels despite 3½pp higher mortgage rates today. The improvement in the available supply of housing should increase the sensitivity of homebuilding to affordability constraints. The market pricing for the October meeting has receded a lot. By the time of writing, just 2-3bps were priced, down from pricing of 12.5bps a month ago; events in France might have contributed to this. We stick to our forecast of a December hike, to 2.75%. Inflation peak at/above 4% in early 2027 to prompt ECB hike to 3% The inflation outlook has gradually worsened in recent weeks. September inflation was higher than expected, at 3.8% y/y, but we think the peak in inflation is still ahead of us, in January 2027, when we expect a rate of 4%. However, depending on geopolitical events and their potential implications on energy prices, inflation could be even higher at that stage. Against this background, we now expect the ECB to hike rates by another 25bps to 3% in Q1-27. While this hike could happen already on 4 February (right after the release of January inflation), we favour 18 March as the date of the hike. We see two-sided risk for our new call of rates peaking at 3%: Rates might peak already at 2.75% if events in France or the broader tightening in financial conditions via higher bond yields convinced the ECB to stop earlier

The strategies we outlined in the paper generally have shown a positive backtest, but most of the study was conducted on outright trades (US 2y and US 10 y). We now repeat the same exercise but focusing on the 2s10s and 5s30s US curves. The ‘No Memory’ strategy (i.e. trading based solely on the signals generated by the most recent data projection) appears to be the most profitable (Figure 2). Market performance reflects this tension between resilient fundamentals and rising risk concerns. Since the OAT-driven rates sell-off began, investment grade credit has materially outperformed other segments of the European credit market on a beta-adjusted basis ( Figure 2). High yield, leveraged loans and subordinated financial instruments have lagged most notably, while corporate hybrids have also underperformed despite comparatively stable corporate fundamentals. In our view, this divergence increasingly reflects investor caution rather than a sharp deterioration in issuer quality. With concerns ranging from EU-China trade disputes and elevated rates to AI-related uncertainty and growing high yield dispersion, there is certainly no shortage of potential catalysts for risk aversion. Yet positioning matters. As discussed in our CRV section, the short- risk base in Main remains notable, creating an attractive backdrop for owning receivers and bullish risk-reversal structures. We view these as particularly effective overlays for cash portfolios that remain modestly underweight credit risk versus benchmark. By contrast, we continue to favour hedges expressed through Xover, where idiosyncratic high yield risks remain elevated and where the apparent short-risk positioning may be overstating genuine bearish conviction due to ongoing tranche-related hedging activity. Together, these measures raise an obvious question: how much additional diesel could reach the market, and what would that mean for prices? The answer depends less on the size of the announcement than on the government's willingness to deliver the promised barrels and, crucially, how much of this supply would be genuinely incremental. That is, of course, if Europe actually releases the barrels. records.text: Drivers of G4 Term Premium Our estimates of term premium suggest that term premia have risen substantially over the last half decade, standing around 150-200bp above 2021 levels across the G41. With different drivers cited for the increase, we introduce a new modeling framework to identify what has pushed term premium so much higher (Exhibit 1). Our framework can explain around 70-80% of the recent increase, underlining the mostly fundamental nature of the selloff. That said, about 35-50bp remain unexplained in each market, pointing to room for long-end yields to move lower should the macro backdrop change and skew of risks shift. Theory suggests that greater macro uncertainty, especially around the path of growth, inflation, and policy, raise the duration risks that investors bear when holding longer-term over shorter-term bonds. Consequently, they demand higher term premium to hold that risk. Since the pandemic, dispersion across macro forecasts (which we use to measure uncertainty) has risen notably across the G4, reflecting the effects of higher inflation, shifting central bank approaches, geopolitical risks, and the implications of the AI buildout. At the same time, greater bond supply erodes the convenience value investors typically assign to sovereign bonds given the increased availability, in turn raising term premium. S&P puts greater emphasis on standalone capital strength, with callable capital from AAA members providing an additional buffer. France is therefore a more direct rating input under Moody’s than under Fitch or S&P . The main downside risks are therefore broader than France alone: Moody’s highlights a German downgrade, multi-notch deterioration among highly rated shareholders, a systemic crisis or waning shareholder support ; Fitch similarly focuses on deterioration in callable capital from highly rated shareholders, particularly if ESM lending expands materially. The ESM also benefits from an unusually explicit legal backstop. Callable capital is an irrevocable and unconditional shareholder obligation; in an emergency, the Managing Director can call capital without prior governing-body approval, with payment due within seven days. If one shareholder fails to pay, additional pro-rata calls can be made on the remaining members within their callable-capital commitments. Compared with the EU, the ESM therefore has fewer supporting sovereigns but a more explicit contractual capital-support mechanism. OAT-Bund spreads: directionality, cheapness, risks ahead Among field trip participants, there was broad agreement on the fact that part of the widening in OAT-Bund spreads had to do with the rise in the overall level of EUR rates, given the higher financing costs weighed on interest expenses and thereby made the budgetary equation more complicated. Interest expenditure is also a metric that rating agencies focus on but those could still argue that France’s elevated weighted average maturity of debt means that higher yields would have to persist for longer to have a meaningful impact on total interest burden. OAT-Bund spreads were seen to incorporate some cheapness related to recent technical flows (eg. stop losses on long ASW positions), but clients noted that the length of the budgetary process, the positioning for increased supply in Q1 and election uncertainty could limit appetite to fade this cheapness. ECB action in case of renewed widening was seen by clients to be focused on verbal intervention, with slowing of QT as next step but considered at much wider levels and under contagion to other EGBs. Our baseline of a 100-150bp range for 10y OAT-Bunds in the next few months was seen as optimistic by clients, although many thought peak uncertainty and pressure would be later in 1Q27.

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Oil Tracker: Running out of buffers Our baseline outlook for the U.S. economy assumes a permanent oil risk premium. The renewed pressure on energy prices has dragged the world into the seventh month of this prolonged energy price shock. Historically, episodes of acute geopolitical or physical supply disruption have mostly lasted 3–6 months, with the notable exception of the 1978–79 oil shock and its aftermath. As buffers such as higher U.S. exports, weaker Chinese imports, and ample inventories begin to fade, we update our oil tracker to highlight developments and trends that matter for U.S. economic growth. The latest data suggest that crude oil inventories in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) have fallen further, while both U.S. crude oil imports and exports have remained on an upward trend. Crude oil prices have continued to rise, while diesel margins have widened further. SSW events disrupt the polar vortex, driving high-pressure blocking over Europe and prolonged low-wind spells . records.text: M Idea 2 Quality Breaks Out; What's Next? We have been arguing for several months that the market is moving from an early-cycle recovery led by lower-quality stocks into a more selective mid-cycle environment where earnings durability matters more. That transition is becoming clearer beneath the index. Earnings remain strong, but the rise in rates and the more hawkish policy path priced since Jackson Hole have compressed valuations across much of the market. As a result, the S&P 500 continues to look more resilient than the average stock, while leadership has been shifting toward the higher-quality companies we have been recommending. One of the clearest signs is the recent performance of our composite quality factor. It has risen to a new 52-week high, surpassing its late-July peak (Exhibit 1 ). The move is particularly notable because quality lagged during the final leg of the summer rally. Since the equal-weight S&P 500 peaked on Aug. 14, our quality long-short composite has gained ~6%. The improvement has been broad across the quality sub-composites, led by profitability, as investors are being more selective about the companies that can sustain earnings, margins and cash flow through higher financing costs. Key to our call is the recognition that Liberation Day in April 2025 marked the end of the rolling recession and the beginning of a new economic cycle--a time when low quality outperforms. We set the number of variables to pick from the pool of candidates to three to avoid overfitting, preserve simplicity of interpretation and limit computational costs. As of 2023, 70% of transmission lines and transformers deployed on the grid were over 25 years old. In response, U.S. utilities are projected to invest $239 billion in 2026 to make the grid stronger and more reliable, per EEI. As a result, we see the midterm elections as having a relatively benign impact for most regulated utilities as critical infrastructure investment continues. However, we see more nuanced impacts state-by-state for the merchant IPP generators, particularly in regions with high power demand and significant community pushback on data center development, such as in PJM and ERCOT. A resurgence in energy prices now places global CPI on track to rise at a 5%ar in the three months through October. Central bankers initially displayed patience in the face of the energy sector shock, recognizing its likely transitory nature as well as its threat to growth. However, the shock’s persistence and growth resilience have shifted them from their earlier easing bias to outright hikes. The tightening has been limited, with global policy rates outside China only 17bp higher than at the start of the year. Caution should remain intact through year-end. records.text: The securitization rate during 1H’2026 was roughly unchanged vs. 2025 levels In contrast to the trend observed over the past few years, agency MBS securitization rates in 1H’26 were roughly in line with 2025 levels (Exhibit 3). We attribute this apparent stabilization primarily to a shift in loan composition toward refinance loans, which have historically exhibited higher securitization rates than purchase loans (Exhibit 4). As the refinance share increased in 1H’26 relative to 2025, it provided a compositional boost to the aggregate securitization rate. Controlling for this mix shift, purchase-loan securitization rates declined in 1H’26, broadly continuing the trend of the prior few years. If the recent back-up in mortgage rates persists into 2027 and the share of refinance loans declines, we expect the securitization rate in 2027 to dip relative to 2026 levels. A decline in the agency MBS securitization rate should be a modest positive for non-agency RMBS issuance volume. RMBS 2027 issuance is likely to surpass 2026’s post-GFC record Aggregate non-agency RMBS issuance volume has already matched 2026’s full-year high, surpassing $207 billion through mid-October on the back of historic non-QM issuance. This heavy pace of issuance highlights the steady growth in the share of non-agency RMBS across total residential mortgage securitizations, with 2026 on track to set a new post-GFC high (Exhibit 5). The current El Niño tracking toward its peak historically drives windier conditions across Northwestern Europe, which should support a near-term recovery in wind generation and weigh on power prices . Once El Niño peaks, the key downside risk to generation is Sudden Stratospheric Warming, which could replicate or worsen the late-Q3 volatility. SSW events disrupt the polar vortex, driving high-pressure blocking over Europe and prolonged low-wind spells . Gas prices to peak in November: Our base case assumes gas prices peak around November, after which multiple supply-side offsets should ease winter balances (see Oil, gas and gasoil forecast update: Winter whirlwind, 8 September). This underpins our bearish power view to the market, though the outlook remains sensitive to cold snap risks in Q1. El Niño weighs on demand, structural tailwinds provide a floor: We see competing forces shaping European power demand towards year end. As we discussed in our recent global inflation deep dive, the oil bottleneck has shifted downstream from crude availability toward refining capacity and petroleum-product balances. Higher gasoline prices feed rapidly into headline inflation, while diesel presents a broader risk through transportation, logistics, agriculture, construction and other intermediate inputs. The longer the shock persists, the greater the probability that higher producer costs eventually reach core consumer prices. Canada remains relatively well insulated against broader pass-through. Domestic crude production, refining capacity and natural gas supply reduce the risk that higher international energy prices become a physical supply constraint. More importantly, the economy continues to operate with considerable excess supply, and we expect more of the adjustment to occur through margins and real spending rather than a sustained acceleration in core inflation. records.text: ab 19 October 2026 Global Research European Rates Strategy European supras: not all France risk is created equal Key takeaways  France sensitivity differs materially across European supras . An isolated French downgrade is unlikely to trigger downgrades of ESM, EIB, EBRD or CEB, where stand-alone financial strength, diversification and/or callable capital provide meaningful buffers. EFSF is the clear exception , given its more concentrated sovereign-guarantee structure and France’s importance within it.  EFSF has the clearest direct rating link to France. S&P and Fitch have already downgraded EFSF following a downgrade of France. Moody’s still rates EFSF Aaa, but with a negative outlook reflecting France’s negative outlook, making the 23 October France review a near-term catalyst.  Legal and capital structures drive France sensitivity. EFSF’s guarantee- based model creates the most direct transmission, while standalone capital and callable-capital buffers limit the impact at ESM, EIB, EBRD and CEB; the EU relies instead on its budget and own-resources framework.  Stay cautious on EFSF; prefer EU on relative value. Current spreads do not, in our view, fully compensate for EFSF’s more direct exposure to French rating risk. Further France rating pressure could catalyse EFSF widening versus EU and peers. From airfares to core goods So far, the clearest evidence of energy pass-through into core CPI has been in airfares, which are running approximately 23% higher than a year ago. This is consistent with our historical estimates, which identify airfares as the category with the strongest response to oil price shocks. Beyond airfares, however, the direct evidence of energy-related price pressures has been much less pronounced. We think this could change over the coming months. There are two main channels through which higher energy costs could increasingly affect core goods prices. The first is through energy-intensive production processes, particularly in categories such as motor vehicles and related products. The second, and potentially more important channel in the current environment, is transportation and distribution. Diesel prices have risen by even more than crude oil prices, increasing the cost of freight transportation across the economy. There are already some warning signs that these pressures are building. Start with the level. The 20y touched 3.985% on October 6, just short of the 4% handle, then retraced 14bp to 3.844% (Wednesday's close) on lower US yields, softer equities and the clean October auctions. That is just 5bp below the 3.895% close of the previous auction day (September 15) — but with the direction reversed: September's auction came mid- selloff, three business days before the hike; this one arrives mid-retracement, with little pre-auction concession — a purer test of demand. records.text: aver, UBS We expect the FOMC's decision to skip October reflects two things, one is the proximity of the mid-term elections and the second is the nature of the inflation problem that the FOMC faces. The problem is not rising inflation, nor an overheating economy. The problem is that 3% inflation is not headed toward 2% sufficiently obviously or fast, depending on which FOMC participant one is listening to. If inflation were more persistently rising and pressure mounting, there would be more urgency to raise rates in October too. Instead, most FOMC participants' communications during the intermeeting period appeared to reflect their Summary of Economic Projections submissions, where even the most hawkish participant thought only one or two more rate hikes, in addition to the September rate hike, would be appropriate over the next four years. In market pricing, once the October skip communications were in place, the expectation of an every meeting pace moderated, the front end rate move looked more contained, and we expect that was welcomed by most FOMC participants. That does not mean rate hikes may not resume at some point if inflation fails to soften but we suspect, at the moment, the Bank of England's Huw Pill's metaphor is useful when he said we are not sure we need to climb the Matterhorn as opposed to Table Mountain. records.text: M Idea 2 Inflation is up, but urgency is not September CPI inflation came in above expectations, with headline and core rising 0.6% m/m and 0.3%, respectively. On a years-on-year basis, this left headline CPI up 3.7% and core up 2.6%. In this edition of our Federal Reserve Monitor, we assess the report in the context of our broader thinking on inflation and our outlook for monetary policy. Despite the upside surprise, we believe the Fed will remain on the sidelines in October and raise its policy rate by 25bp in December and again in March for 75bp in total rate hikes. That said, risks skew in the direction of a Fed that needs to show more urgency to address above- target inflation. A multipolar world and a higher resting inflation rate At a high level, the upside surprise to September inflation is another datapoint that validates our long-held view that the US and global economy is being rewired for a multipolar world, a theme we highlighted in our 2026 Year-Ahead Outlook and 2026 Mid- Year Update. We continue to see a shift away from an era of benign globalization toward one defined by rising economic nationalism, intensified geopolitical competition, and strategic resources used as policy tools. The conflict in the Middle East has intensified competition for energy sources and delivery channels in the same way that trade and pandemic shocks reshaped the landscape in prior years. records.text: on post US CPI and 2) our tactical POLLS triggering the critical level. We think one way to cautiously position for the AI trade is through equities vs credit RVs. In short, we think equities offer long convexity exposure to the AI race, as a small number of eventual winners can generate sufficiently large gains to offset weakness elsewhere in the market or broader index. On the other hand, we think credit has the opposite asymmetry where bondholders only receive limited upside if AI investment delivers but remain exposed to the downside if returns disappoint. Reflecting this, in Figure 9 and Figure 10, we compare seven custom AI-themed credit baskets from The High-Grade Beat: Everyone’s an AI Adopter with equity baskets constructed using the same underlying issuers and corresponding weights. Within equities, summer weakness in hyperscalers and software has been offset by strength elsewhere in the AI complex, particularly in hardware and semiconductors. Recent pressure therefore appears to reflect a rotation between AI themes rather than a wholesale reassessment of the investment cycle that allows the broader equity complex to remain comparatively resilient (Global Asset Allocation - House Views July 2026 – From Penalty Kicks to Macro Risks). In contrast, credit has offered less scope for an equivalent offset, with more limited differentiation across baskets as issuance and balance-sheet concerns increasingly become common factors. Box: The methodological details The optimisation of regressors In our estimation approach, we aim to maximise the explanatory power and variation of variables included. We do this by picking the combination of three variables from a pool of candidate market variables that maximises the R-squared of the regression, subject to pairwise correlation and variance inflation factor multicollinearity tests. A challenge with the approach combining R-squared maximisation and multicollinearity tests is that the optimisation process might pick up a combination of variables for a given sovereign that makes little intuitive sense from an economic perspective. An example would be trying to explain the variation in the spread of a LatAm country using US corporate credit spreads and EU cyclical versus defensive stocks, because US equities are too highly correlated with US credit spreads and therefore would not pass a strict pairwise correlation test (we set the absolute value threshold at 0.5) should these corporate spreads be included in the regression (Exhibit 5). In contrast, EU equities would be a reasonable enough proxy for US equities and not as highly correlated with US corporate credit spreads. One solution to this ‘optimisation-interpretation’ issue is to allow for a rich enough set of global market variables to choose from to isolate market trends in a way that is as orthogonal as possible (see discussion below on China 5-year CDS). records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 19 Oct 2026 11:26:25 ET │ 14 pages China Economics On Track for 2026, Harder Test in 2027 CITI'S TAKE China's cyclical stabilization is playing out as we expected. GDP growth rebounded to 4.5% YoY in 26Q3, in line with our above-consensus forecast, while September data showed domestic demand running somewhat better than expected. With recent policy efforts still coming through, we maintain our GDP growth forecast at 4.6%YoY for both 26Q4E and 2026E. As growth stays on track to hit this year's target, we expect policymakers to focus on execution while shelving new stimulus. This near-term stabilization doesn't alleviate our concerns about 2027 and beyond, given: [1] an elevated household savings rate signaling weak consumer sentiment; [2] a potentially bigger property drag ahead, even as price signals turn more favorable; and [3] more early signs of new-economy peaking. A policy pivot could be inevitable, and we watch the year-end Politburo meeting and CEWC for the earliest hints (see: Approaching Inflection). China scrap: tighter VAT enforcement has disrupted the domestic collection chain and supports cathode demand China’s scrap disruption, the main tightening driver of our 2026/27 balances, began in early 2026, when tighter enforcement of VAT invoicing requirements disrupted the flow of material through the country’s highly fragmented scrap collection chain. Much of China’s domestic scrap is collected by individuals and small traders who cannot issue VAT invoices themselves, making it difficult for recycling companies to obtain the documentation needed to reclaim VAT on their purchases. To address this problem, China introduced reverse invoicing in 2024, allowing qualified recycling companies to issue invoices on behalf of these sellers. However, stricter enforcement aimed at preventing invoice abuse, together with higher compliance costs and concerns over historical tax records, has made parts of the traditional collection model uneconomic. As a result, physical scrap may still be available, but it has become increasingly difficult and expensive for processors to source material with the required invoices1. Because scrap has typically met around 15% of fabricators’ copper needs, the resulting shortfall has increased China’s reliance on refined copper. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 premium. Globally, financial conditions are introducing tougher questions to the macro landscape. Until last week, the economy’s message had been clear: higher rates were restraining some sectors, but without meaningfully altering the expansion’s trajectory. As long as expected returns rise alongside borrowing costs, then yields can remain high without becoming decisively restrictive. But as our Rates Strategy colleagues have noted, inflationary pressures have pushed up real rates, not breakevens, so the market is telling us that policy is getting tighter to restrain growth and eventually pull down inflation. Last week’s inflation print reinforces this debate. Are financial conditions restrictive? With several catalysts ahead — Q3 earnings, hyperscaler capex, credit spread widening, US elections, OAT spreads, and the Fed meeting — markets will need to shift to assessing growth risks as central banks try to calibrate.

To be clear, we believe the US mid- terms are likely to matter more for fiscal policy, tariffs, regulation, M&A, and rate volatility (via the debt ceiling debate) than corporate fundamentals. While the Democrats are widely anticipated to secure the House (~90% prediction odds), the outcome of the Senate race is expected to be much closer. Currently, there is about ~60-65% likelihood for a Blue Wave depending on which prediction market one focuses on. A Blue Wave scenario would likely shift the policy landscape on the margin, whereas a Gridlock scenario would be beneficial primarily through limited downside policy risk rather than creating a new upside catalyst. While investor concern for the midterms has largely centered on the pace of the AI/datacenter buildout, we expect AI capex momentum to remain intact after the midterms and potentially even strengthen in 2027 and 2028. For leveraged finance, the impact of the election outcome will likely be more nuanced and favor credit picking. Political willingness: a longer-term risk Political pressure on member-state support is already becoming more explicit. Marine Le Pen has proposed materially reducing France’s contribution to the EU budget, including cuts as early as 2027. However, existing multiannual commitments are legally binding, making a unilateral reduction problematic; the 2028–34 MFF negotiations provide the more relevant avenue for changing France’s contribution over the longer term. Resistance to further fiscal integration is also visible in Germany. In a recent live interview with The Economist, AfD's Alice Weidel argued for a less integrated EU and expressed strong scepticism towards further common European financing. The timing provides an important buffer: Germany’s next federal election is not due until 2029, by which point the 2028–34 MFF should already be in place , making any major policy shift more relevant for subsequent budgets and common borrowing. Less fiscal integration, however, need not mean weaker credit: a smaller EU policy remit could mean fewer programmes and less issuance. It becomes a rating concern only if political resistance starts to constrain resources available for debt service or weakens the agencies’ assumptions around extraordinary member-state support. The range of possible outcomes should not be framed simply as supportive or restrictive for the industry. Reflexivity is real in commodity markets, and all else equal (which is a very bad assumption for a global commodity), ‘supportive’ policy tends to drive hydrocarbon costs lower, while ‘restrictive’ policy tends to drive prices higher. US Energy policy decisions have historically been less about binary outcomes than trying to tip the proverbial scales on incentives. Policies that accelerate permitting, expand access to federal acreage, or provide greater regulatory certainty could improve project economics and shorten development timelines, while tighter emissions standards, higher royalty or bonding requirements, or narrower access to federal lands could raise compliance costs and constrain activity. Lastly, we can re-express this implied volatility premium being priced into swap- tions in terms of number of incremental days of additional volatility. For example, on Oct 5th, 1Mx10Y closed at 6.9 bp/day versus an expected 6.7 bp/day (based on changes in 2W expiry implied vols). Given ~21 business days over the 1M horizon, we can say that the total squared volatility represented by experiencing a 6.9 bp/day over 21 business days is the same as experiencing the originally expected 6.7 bp/day for a slightly longer period of 22.5 days. In this sense, the implied vol premium can be thought of as representing 1.5 additional volatility days. The table suggests that the midterm premium priced into the options markets is relatively constant across various tails, and is around 1-1.5 days, much low- er relative to the election premium from 2024 (The election enters the hearts and minds of options traders, Interest Rate Derivatives, US Fixed Income Markets Weekly, 5/10/2024). We also explore how implieds trade around midterms. We find that longer-expiry vols tend to decline as we approach and get past midterm elections, likely reflecting event premium getting taken out (Figure 13). With not much event premium priced in, we con- tinue to prefer soft bearish expressions in the upper-right side and recommend main- taining shorts in 6Mx30Y versus 1Yx30Y. There appears to be more consensus on a tougher stance toward China, and the recent agreement of a cap on imports of hybrid vehicles suggests diplomatic solutions can still be found. That said, this does not solve underlying competitiveness issues, for which we think more progress on implementing aspects of the Draghi and Letta reports is key. Given the negative outlook, worse-than-expected growth data and rising pressure on the deficit, a rating downgrade to A1 (stable outlook) seems more likely than not. records.text: funds' exposure to the high yield market has remained broadly stable over the past year. Across our sample of approximately 30 large IG fund managers, the median fund continues to allocate just over 5% of assets to high yield, predominantly BB-rated, credit. We estimate this translates into roughly 3.5% of the broader PE HY market. Several competing forces likely explain this stability, in our view. A subdued fallen angel pipeline limited the addition of 'incidental' BB holdings to IG portfolios, while higher all-in yields reduced the incentive to move down the credit curve, particularly with parts of HY screening rich on a relative value basis. Where allocations did increase, we suspect they were tilted towards corporate hybrids, particularly given the substantial wave of BB-rated hybrid issuance seen earlier this year. ECB: 0-1% (unchanged) The ECB’s already small HY footprint continues to shrink as it unwinds its corporate bond purchase programmes, with holdings now estimated at just 0.3% of the market. This year’s decline reflects a combination of maturities, calls and sales following downgrades. While fallen angels (eg, Lanxess and INWIT) have extended the remaining high yield portfolio’s maturity profile, a meaningful share of residual HY holdings is due to mature in 2027. Barring another wave of large fallen angels, we expect the ECB’s footprint to shrink further next year as these holdings run off naturally. A decelerating growth backdrop usually supports the outperformance of stocks with secular earnings growth over those with cyclical growth profiles. During recent decades, Info Tech and Health Care have typically performed best when growth was positive but decelerating. Cyclical sectors such as Materials and Consumer Discretionary have fared worst. Among equity factors, stocks with price momentum, positive earnings revisions, and low volatility have typically outperformed in decelerating growth environments. Heading into 2027, we expect investors will assign a scarcity premium to companies with accelerating EPS growth and positive EPS revisions. In contrast with the historical growth cycle playbook, extremely narrow market breadth suggests that investors should be wary of Momentum factor risk today. records.text: Germany In Germany, the final print confirmed the composite PMI at 53.8 in September, a level slightly above February. The manufacturing output index stands at a healthy 56.0, although the signal from the ifo was slightly less upbeat. The services index rose sharply to 52.9, despite penalising seasonal factors. High-frequency data has been weak on net into October. On the soft side, high-frequency consumer confidence stabilised in the first half of October, possibly reflecting policy interventions moderating the consumer price of fuels, but remains at soft levels. The consumer survey of the Retail Federation showed a slight moderation in consumer sentiment in October. Flight data and job postings also moderated in early October. Other indicators, including truck toll mileage and mortgage growth, moved broadly sideways. On the more positive side, the Bundesbank’s Weekly Activity Index rose sharply in early October after underperforming PMIs and hard data for most of this year. On net, we keep our forecast close to the model-implied prediction for a moderation in the composite index to 53.3, reflecting a moderation in services activity and broadly unchanged manufacturing output. Investment potential of the ETS reform Because the allocation of free allowances is linked to strict investment obligations, exporters will experience only minor short -term relief. In what is already a challenging economic and structural environment, companies must provide substantial upfront financial resources in order to receive free allocations. For industrial sectors whose products, using lower-emission production methods, are not price-competitive on the global market against more carbon -intensively produced goods, investments in decarboni sation will not alter the structural disadvantage in global exports. The Parliament's draft does not solve this problem either but merely postpones it by a few years. The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, which entered into force in early 2026, does not provide a fundamental remedy. CBAM is intended to impose the same CO₂ costs on imports from third countries as on goods produced within the EU under the Emissions Trading System. However, the system has its weaknesses. Notable among these are the high administrative costs and the risk that the system can be circumvented by importers. records.text: Our thoughts on USD, EUR, ILS, GBP , FX and Terms of Trade & Frontier FX USD: What got you there also got you here. For much of this year, we have n argued that strong US economic and equity performance have been important AI-driven tailwinds to the Dollar. The AI boom has raised capital expenditures and near-term inflationary pressures. With the US disproportionately affected by these channels, this has shifted rate differentials in the Dollar’s favor. We think the broad pattern of FX moves this week is most consistent with elements of this framework now coming under renewed scrutiny, rather than a negative currency reaction to the FOMC’s emphasis that there is no ‘urgency’ to hike at the October meeting (though we still see dovish policy preferences as a more medium-term limitation on the Dollar). The Dollar’s underperformance this week amid renewed AI concerns and a sharp tech sell-off closely resembles the “DeepSeek sell-off” last January, which was also a clear negative Dollar event in real time—the flipside of the US’s outsized exposure to this theme. Notably though, DXY fell by more this time around than it did during the “DeepSeek episode” despite less US equity underperformance. We think this largely reflects an element of rate relief in European assets. records.text: 12 Europe Economic Weekly | 16 October 2026 National recovery plan: final stretch, but no fiscal cliff in 2027 In September 2026, Italy formally submitted its request for the tenth and final payment, worth €28.4bn. The request marks the completion of the implementation phase of Italy's €194.4bn Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP). To unlock the final tranche, Italy reported the achievement of 156 milestones and targets, bringing the total number of completed RRP objectives to 576. Given the sheer size of the final tranche, expectations in Rome are that the European Commission's assessment could take longer than previous reviews, with the actual disbursement potentially extending beyond the end of 2026. Implementation has progressed further, but official data remain scarce. As of February 2026, actual spending had reached €113.3bn, up from €104.6bn at end-2025, equivalent to around 58% of the total RRP envelope (Exhibit 8). At the same time, government administrations estimated that approximately €24.2bn of planned expenditure, largely related to infrastructure projects, will be shifted beyond the 2026 deadline. In practice, this means that fiscal support from EU funds is likely to continue even after the formal completion of the RRP. Equally important, the risk of a fiscal cliff over our forecast horizon appears limited amid the deployment of other EU funds. Markets are pricing an 89% probability of a Fed hike and a shallow rate hike cycle of additional 100bp of tightening over the next year. The aftereffects of a hot European summer have hampered the recovery of French nuclear availability into the shoulder season, driven by a combination of low river levels and low flow rates leading to cooling-related outages at various reactors. In late September, EDF announced that output at its Civaux power plant could be temporarily reduced from 1 October due to low flow rates of the Vienne River, and at the start of this month, the Civaux 1 and Civaux 2 reactors suffered short-lived forced outages of around 1GW due to “environmental issues”. The return of Chooz 1 and Chooz 2 – which have been out due to river cooling issues since July – have also been constantly delayed, with the plants now expected to return only on 30 October. Average availability was just 57% in the first week of October compared with 69% in the same period last year. Risks of further outages: Nuclear plants near the Garonne, Moselle and Meuse rivers appear most exposed to forced outages in our view, as the Week 42 averages for those rivers were 72%, 51% and 43% below their five-year averages, respectively (Figure 4). We hence think the Chooz plant outage is likely to be extended into November

Nominal growth held steady at 6.0%YoY, the highest since 22Q1, as PPI hit a new high in September. September numbers pointed to somewhat better-than-expected domestic demand. The supply side and the new economy remained supportive, unsurprisingly, with exports growth running at 36.3%YoY and industrial production at 5.5%YoY (Citi/Mkt: 5.2/5.5%YoY) – high-tech IP continued expanding at 15.3%YoY. We had argued that August could mark the cyclical bottom, and domestic demand indeed improved from September: retail sales rose to 1.1%YoY, the highest reading since April, and investment growth also appeared to have bottomed, with monthly FAI growth estimated at -7.2%YoY vs. -10.6%YoY in August. We expect policymakers to stay in execution mode given the latest data. Cumulative growth reached 4.6% YoY in 26Q1-3, comfortably within this year's 4.5–5% target range. A 4.3% print in 26Q4 – aided by a low base from 25Q4 – would be enough to secure the full-year number, so new stimulus such as a rate cut or budget revision is off the table in our view. Despite September's stabilization, the long-awaited reversal of fiscal austerity has yet to materialize, as hinted by earlier credit and deposit data.
