records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 29 3Q Systematic Earnings (Full MS Coverage) Summary: • Previews: KPI previews are +18% vs +24% net positive last quarter and NTM EPS previews are +15% vs +27% last quarter on projected NTM impacts. Previews are currently net positive across all sectors with the exception of Industrials. 3Q Preview Tracking Our Morgan Stanley Analysts submit a systematic earnings preview where they forecast two items: 1) KPI and 2) NTM EPS impact. Below we summarize the sector and industry summaries of these previews. The population is the Morgan Stanley US coverage, which is broader than the S&P 500 and roughly similar to the Russell 1000. Methodology: Each analyst identifies the key performance indicator (KPI) for each individual stock and it may differ from NTM EPS. For example, the KPI for a Financial Services or Semiconductor company may be net assets or GPU demand and this may differ from NTM EPS (although, it is often similar). records.text: ab 19 October 2026 Global Research Global Strategy Private Credit: Higher Rates Meet Refinancing Risk Executive summary Private credit maturity walls are more front-loaded than those in leveraged loans, but should only become a meaningful test from mid-2027, when technology refinancing needs begin to rise. The wall is disproportionately populated by weaker 2020-21 vintages and software loans, increasing the risk that refinancing at higher spreads becomes a catalyst for further deterioration. Current interest coverage suggests that higher rates alone should be manageable, but the margin for error is thin, particularly in technology if earnings growth weakens materially. We see US private credit default rates rising by an incremental 3% over the next 12 months, with contributions from stressed refi and software sectors. However, we view an AI disruption-driven earnings shock as the key upside risk to defaults: a sustained 10% annualized decline in technology EBITDA would push the sector's median US and European ICR below 1.0x by late-2028. We expect refinancing to increasingly become the forcing mechanism for weaker credits, driving more bifurcated outcomes as stronger borrowers retain access to capital while weaker credits face higher spreads, tighter terms or restructuring. Maturity walls are looming. Tech stress should be deferred but not defused Private credit’s maturity wall is front-loaded, but technology stress may not resurface until Q2’27. However, the US is also in the midst of the AI spending boom that could be fueling demand-side price pressures. In our view, the US economy shows few signs of overt overheating, particularly in the labor market where employment growth remains subdued and wage growth is decelerating despite a low unemployment rate and solid productivity gains. We believe the high import content of hyperscaler capex spending is more likely to fuel positive output gaps and price pressures abroad, particularly in Asia, than at home. Nonetheless, real consumer spending is growing at a reasonably solid pace, and the consumer has held up despite a rising cost of living. The economy may not be showing signs of overheating now, but they could emerge with a lag. A measured recalibration of policy still seems likely The sources of inflation matter for the outlook for monetary policy. Traditional economic analysis says the central bank is most effective at leaning against the second-round effects of supply shocks, as opposed to reacting to changes in headline inflation. Yet if inflation is increasingly being driven by demand-side forces, then monetary policy has a clearer role. Most FOMC participants that gave their view during the inter-meeting period have said they do not see an aggressive rate hike cycle as appropriate. records.text: M Update 2 October Prepays Forecast It's been a slow end of summer for prepays. September speeds slowed 8% for 30-year conventionals and 11% for Ginnies, driven by higher lagged mortgage rates and waning seasonality. Many of the same themes will continue through fall. We forecast headline October speeds declining 10% for 30y conventionals, 10% for 15y conventionals, and 16% for Ginnies. The slowing is expected across the stack, though higher coupon Ginnies are expected to see the largest declines as shorter lags realize the effects of higher mortgage rates more quickly. Lower coupon speeds are forecasted to slow ~10% with lock-in and seasonal effects. We've pointed out that turnover tends to closely follow existing home sale activity, which our housing strategists expect to decelerate into 7%+ mortgage rates. Moving forward into November, lagged mortgage rates will continue to rise, seasonal effects will weaken into winter, and daycount will fall by 3 days. We expect speeds to continue their deceleration across the stack. For the specific cohorts underlying our aggregate forecasts, see Appendix – Agency MBS October Prepays Forecast. The Bank of Korea will publish a separate issue note in the October MPB regarding the conditions for a recovery in private consumption, which could provide a clue for gauging the timing and pace of future policy rate hikes. We retain our neutral stance on the KRW. The market is currently pricing in roughly one more hike, taking the terminal rate to 3.25% (Figure 3). We believe such pricing is reasonable given core inflation is in the mid-to-high 2% range. Unless the October MPB meeting delivers a third consecutive hike, we expect KRW to be driven by flows. KRW remains strong relative to other EM currencies thanks to exporters’ consistent USD selling. That said, Korean institutional and retail investors’ purchases of foreign equities continue due to the stronger performance of U.S. and global equities relative to the KOSPI (Figure 4). We see the low-1,300s as an attractive entry point for a long USDKRW position (vs. 1,331 as of Oct 19). The Aerospace & Defense subsector has benefited from trade policy developments with significant international contract wins, particularly in commercial aerospace. For Aerospace & Defense we do not expect the outcome of mid-term elections to have a material impact on the sector’s favorable trends in the near- and medium- term. In commercial aerospace we expect new aircraft demand, higher OEM production rates, and global travel demand to drive growth. To date, demand for commercial aftermarket has not been significantly impacted by higher fuel costs and reduced airline capacity due to the conflicts in the Middle East and we expect this end market to remain resilient. On the defense side, we acknowledge that there is risk related to the defense spending outlook. With a change in Congress, large budget increases like the current defense budget request of $1.5 trillion could be scaled back, which would have implications on the broader industry. We could also see certain high-profile priorities for the current administration delayed or scaled back like the Golden Dome and the F-47 programs. Throughout the past 4 years we have consistently argued that the UK's labour market malaise stems from cyclical roots. While financial conditions remain tight - thus likely weighing on job intentions in the more domestically-oriented sectors - global growth tailwinds are likely aiding sentiment in manufacturing and higher value-added services sectors. All in all, as risks to our growth forecasts are now more balanced, so are our views on the labour market from here. In addition, despite the rising demand headwind of AI on graduate hiring in particular, we remain of the more constructive view that more productive workers are a more appealing proposition for employers as well. We are also hesitant to see any AI-related hit to demand as structural - workers impacted by AI, in our view, are younger and with fairly transferable skills, and so any potential re-training frictions might not be that large. UK macro discourse has had a strong tendency to see any demand hit in recent years as a structural phenomena - NICs hike, AI - and we continue to reside on the other side of this argument. For now, however, we see vacancies that have been very stagnant and a public sector where payrolls momentum ought to cool a bit. Under EDP, France has to tighten its primary structural balance by 0.5%-pt next year (beyond 2027, France has to tighten the structural balance by 0.5%-pt per year, i.e. includ- ing interest expenses). This trajectory is formalized through a primary net expenditure trajectory. France needs to keep the growth rate of primary net spending in nominal terms below 1.2%. In our view, achieving such a degree of fiscal tightening next year will be difficult given the current political uncertainty. The Lower House in France remains divided and a compro- mise needs to be struck for the budget to become law (proba- bly after article 49.3 is invoked). The government may, once again, have to a resort to the “special law” (i.e. rolling the 2026 budget into 2027). An alternative, never used so far, would be to pass the budget by ordinance if the discussion in the House is not conclusive. Importantly, the government argued that the measures pre- sented in the budget draft could easily be tweaked or removed by the next government, in our view lowering the bar for the budget to become law. But reaching a 5.0% deficit next year will be difficult. We assume a 5.2% deficit for 2027, after a 5.4% deficit this year. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 The latest leg of the equity market sell-off provides a complementary signal. The sell-off now suggests weakness has begun migrating from the broader market up into the leadership that had previously insulated the index. • Narrow breadth makes an index more vulnerable when investors reduce exposure to dominant constituents, particularly when those positions share similar fundamental drivers, financing requirements, and risk exposures. The combination of credit and equity weakness suggests transmission of tight financial conditions is becoming more visible in assets sensitive to the marginal cost of capital. Treasuries en vogue as risk-off hedges One of the more important developments has been the response of US Treasuries. From 2022 to 2024, investors increasingly questioned the hedging properties of US Treasuries. During this time, weekly returns of the US Treasury Index correlated positively with the returns on riskier assets, such as the S&P 500 Index and the US High-Yield Index. • If the S&P 500 Index delivered a negative return, then so too did the US Treasury Index — rendering Treasuries a poor hedging instrument. But through most of 2025, Treasury returns correlated negatively to those of the S&P 500 Index. records.text: 25 Tarek HamidAC (1-212) 834-5468 tarek.x.hamid@jpmorgan.com North America Credit Research 16 October 2026 J P M O R G A N HG & HY Financials For Financials the key consideration is whether a Blue Wave could reverse the deregulation agenda that has been set forth by the Federal Reserve as well as other regulatory agencies. The regulatory environment has eased for banks over the last two years as we have seen several proposals and rules pass that reduced capital requirements, reduced stress test volatility, enabled banks to expand their balance sheets, and, importantly, encouraged consolidation among regional banks. This deregulation agenda has allowed banks to expand ROTCE which has resulted in higher equity prices and tighter spreads. The deregulation agenda and policy is adminstered by the Federal Reserve, and there is little evidence that the current will be altered with a blue wave. The Fed recently finalized its changes to the stress test process, providing more transparency and reducing capital variability over time. We view the outcome as credit positive since sharp movements in capital requirements in every test increases uncertainty and forces management teams to hold a buffer over a buffer. We await the finalization of the Basel 3 end game and proposals on liquidity ratios. We don’t think any of these proposals will be impacted by the mid-term elections. However, a divided Congress or a Blue Wave would definitely reduce consolidation activity within regional banks.

records.text: Global Equity Strategy 19 October 2026 ab 23 Global Equity Strategy UBS Research Regions and countries: looking for underpriced growth As discussed earlier, we want to be positioned in the near-term for rates staying elevated while avoiding short duration exposure as there is a good chance rates eventually normalise. We have highlighted that the market is pricing in lower growth and/or lower profitability for many areas of the market relative to consensus expectations in the US (see Multiple Gaps) and globally (see Broadening Growth, Pricing Doubt). Look for low PEG ratios, strong revisions amid rate sensitivity We compare P/E to 2yr forward EPS growth PEG ratios to 3mo earnings momentum for regions and countries. The US, the Netherlands, Taiwan and Korea offer an attractive mix of growth at a discount and relatively strong positive earnings revisions. The UK, Sweden, Canada, India and France are the least attractive market with high PEGs and weaker revisions. Switzerland and Japan have relatively strong earnings revisions but do not look cheap while China and Germany have an an attractive PEG but subdued earnings revisions. India and Korea are also both the most negatively exposed to higher yields on our REVS yield beta which makes the pair trade particularly attractive as it would perform well in a normalised yield environment . The index tends to be negatively serially correlated from month to month but has generally trended up since the beginning of 2025. Adjusted to ISM weights, the index rose 4.1 points to 57.8, with strong gains in the new orders and shipments indexes. Like the headline index, both of these subindexes can be volatile. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures Issuance has been elevated this year: HGB supply in 2026 has been particularly heavy, driven by three factors: ▪ The cash deficit target has been revised up by more than HUF2,000bn to HUF7,230bn. Heavy pre-election spending has weighed on budget execution and the previous government's projections assumed nearly 10% nominal GDP growth. ▪ The government has pre-financed around HUF2,000bn of RRF spending. Spending on these projects began in August, while the matching EU disbursements are not expected until December. In our view, this timing mismatch has been funded through both higher HGB and T-bill issuance. ▪ The finance ministry has lifted its cash balance from HUF5,000bn to around HUF6,000bn (Figure 13), pushing net issuance above what the cash deficit alone would imply. Taken together, gross HGB issuance is set to come in around HUF2,000bn above the original 2026 plan (Figure 11). Net issuance is set to halve: We expect net HGB issuance to fall by around 50% next year, to HUF1,400bn from HUF2,700bn in 2026. The left panel of Exhibit 3 shows that more than 95% of mortgage borrowers—which represent roughly 60% of homeowners—have interest rates below current market rates, and 65% have rates more than 2pp below market rates. The combination of mortgage borrowers refinancing at low rates en masse in 2020 and 2021 and the high current level of mortgage rates has created a significant financial cost to moving, as buying a new home would require homebuyers to prepay their current mortgage and take out a new mortgage at a significantly higher rate. As a result of this “lock-in” effect, we expect existing home sales to total just 3.9mn in 2027, 26% below 2019 levels and modestly below our forecast of 4.0mn for 2026. Beyond next year, we expect existing home sales to gradually edge higher, reflecting the natural decay of the lock-in effect that comes from, for example, borrowers paying down their mortgage. Hyper-ventilating again With both rate and equity volatility higher this week, it’s no surprise that HG spreads are retesting recent wides with JULI +4bp to 96bp. Additionally, the renewed focus on AI fund- ing stress is pushing hyperscaler spreads back towards the summer wides and therefore also leading to a meaningful pickup in broader dispersion. However, the impetus for much of this risk off move was the hot CPI print on Wednesday which got investors concerned the Fed would tighten policy more rapidly than expected, with knock on consequences for the seg- ments of the economy most in need of incremental debt (HY neoclouds, and by implication HG hyperscalers). But fast forward to the end of the week and markets are in fact pricing in the same odds of a Fed hike this month as at the start of the week (17%) and HG yields have somewhat mysteriously dropped 22bp WTD (our rates colleagues offer several theo- ries on why here). Had yields spiked higher post CPI, we’d probably see little reason to stay constructive on HG spreads near term. But this paradoxical reality instead leaves us still constructive: Yields stabilizing near the highs is good for returns and thus demand, especial- ly from the mutual fund universe which just registered its largest outflow since April 2025. records.text: Please ref er to important inf ormation at the end of the report and MAR disclosures 16 October 2026 Political momentum: UK–EU ETS linkage remains the single most important driver of UKA prices . Over the past few weeks, a sequence of positive political developments has materially improved sentiment. On 29 September, Prime Minister AndyBurnham signalled a strengthening UK–EU relationship and opened debate on longer-term alignment, including the possibility of rejoining the single market. While we do not expect this to materialise in the near term, we view the shift as directionally supportive for sentiment around the linkage of the ETSs. Around the same time, the contentious question of UK inclusion in the EU's Made in Europe framework under the Industrial Accelerator Act was effectively deferred to 2027, removing a key roadblock that had weighed on the linkage outlook. Most recently, Burnham confirmed in the House of Commons that the UK–EU summit will be held on 20 November, with a longer-term dialogue on the broader relationship to follow. Technical alignment: Beyond politics, practical convergence between the two systems continues. For example, the UK's hydrogen free allocation consultation, which closed on 2 October, proposed changes explicitly designed to align with EU methodology, a step towards greater compatibility ahead of any formal linkage . records.text: Global Equity Strategy 19 October 2026 ab 15 Own low PEG industries with positive revisions Buying earnings growth at a reasonable valuation is a proven strategy in this environment. Growth alone has not been enough to offset higher yields when the starting valuation is demanding. Our European team shows that earnings have helped parts of cyclical value, while expensive growth can remain sensitive to the price paid and defensives lack a comparable growth offset. The story in EM is similar. Our team shows that the best performing factors when US real yields rise from high levels are high growth, dividend yield and high ROE while the worse ones are high PE and high leverage. European Semis, Cap Goods and Transport offer both earnings growth at a discount and very strong earnings revisions. Telecoms and Banks also offer an attractive mix of strong revisions and revisions. It is similar in the US with Semis, Mining and Tech Hardware offering the best mix of revisions and PEG. Pharma and Software also look attractive. In other words, while the 2026 mid-term election outcome could influence regulation, industrial policy and consumer-focused legislation, we continue to believe that global growth, interest rates and corporate earnings remain the primary drivers of US credit performance. Unlike presidential elections, the midterms are fundamentally a question of congressional control. Republicans currently control both the House and Senate, meaning the election will determine whether that framework remains intact, shifts toward divided government or moves toward Democratic control of both chambers. The resulting implications for credit are unlikely to be uniform across sectors, but instead flow through a relatively small number of policy transmission channels. Transmission channel #1: Fiscal policy, Deficits and Treasury supply For broad credit markets, the most important election-sensitive variable remains fiscal poli- cy. The key question is not whether deficits remain elevated, but whether the election out- come increases or decreases the willingness of Congress to pursue additional spending ini- tiatives, tax changes or fiscal packages. From a credit perspective, the impact is ultimately expressed through Treasury supply, rates and refinancing conditions. On October 10, news on Chinese DRAM maker CXMT’s advancement in a new cell architecture called ‘4F2‘ was disclosed along with the positive comment by its president that the company plans to roll out a new server-memory product based on ‘4F2‘ architecture by the end of 2026. Since then, the share price of major memory suppliers, including Samsung Electronics (SEC), SK Hynix (Hynix), Micron, SanDisk, Kioxia, and CXMT, fell by 11-26% taking away a total market value of well over US$700bn from the memory complex. We believe there were other reasons as well that likely contributed to the decline (e.g. credit and AI financing concerns, the higher-than-expected CPI, etc.), given CXMT’s share price itself also saw a decline and NAND suppliers such as Kioxia/SanDisk (which are less relevant to this technology) also saw large declines. In addition, we also note that DRAM spot pricing, which typically acts as a sentiment indicator in the DRAM market, has continued to trend up throughout the same time period. Nevertheless, in this report we examine the 4F2 technology announced by CXMT and compare the technology/capacity between CXMT and SEC/Hynix in order to examine how much of this news has been potentially priced in. Bottom line, while we believe some concerns on the technology progress are appropriate and the capacity gap is narrowing, we believe there is still a significant technology gap, especially in advanced node DRAM and HBM. Moreover, the lesson from other elections this year has been that FX markets can move substantially on expectations alone before any policy shift is implemented. Nevertheless, we think there are a few reasons not to expect a sustained appreciation of the Shekel. First, current polling points to a tight race between the incumbent and opposition blocs, keeping the odds of an unclear, higher-uncertainty outcome still high. Second, while market perception could shift under different election outcomes, economic policy proposals are relatively similar across the board. Plus, while the judicial reform discussions drove ILS weaker in 2023, it is difficult to argue that there is still a substantial country-specific premium priced in when the Shekel is trading near its strongest levels over the past 30 years. Third, and relatedly, the Bank of Israel has been pushing back against currency appreciation, and we would expect this to still be the case if ILS were to appreciate meaningfully post-elections, especially as inflation dynamics remain quite benign. What is 4F2 - the benefits and costs DRAM is composed of millions of individual memory cells that store electrical charges to represent data signals. In conventional designs, DRAM relies on a 6F² (3F×2F) layout (F represents the reference minimum feature size). By contrast, the 4F² architecture optimizes cell geometry so that each single-bit memory cell occupies an area of just 2F×2F. Because this 4F² layout requires less physical footprint per cell, manufacturers can pack more memory cells into the same die area, achieving higher bit density. However, scaling down to 4F² architecture introduces challenges, as smaller transistors become increasingly susceptible to current leakage from memory cells. To overcome these drawbacks, CXMT plans to integrate VSG (Vertical Surrounding Gate) transistors alongside W2W hybrid bonding. What matters more to us in terms of legislative risk is the fact that the GSEs (Government Sponsors Entities, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac specifically) underwrite ~40% of multifamily loans. As long as the GSEs are active, the rental housing REITs have access to a unique contingent / backstop source of financing not available to most REIT property investors. Furthermore, rental housing REIT leverage typically runs well below 6x (VMRK at 5x, MAA at 4.5x, AMH / INVH at 5.2x and 5.4x, respectively), which on assets that consistently trade at <6% cap rates (>16x multiples) equates to effective LTV leverage of <35%. As interest rates rise, the much more leveraged private rental housing market secured loans remain vulnerable as debt service coverage is stressed. This loan stress could create opportunities for the higher rated (BBB+ to mid A) multifamily REITs we cover, with unique best in class access to capital, to opportunistically purchase distressed assets /portfolios. We would be surprised if additional housing legislation is passed targeting the SFR REITs even under greater Democratic influence in DC given the (somewhat) bipartisan coordination on the ROAD Act. At the Financial Street Forum on October 19, PBOC Governor Pan Gongsheng outlined further reforms to China’s monetary policy framework and announced measures for strengthening financial stability and improving market functioning. The Financial Street Forum in Beijing and the Lujiazui Forum in Shanghai are China’s major annual financial policy conferences, serving as an important platform for senior financial regulators to communicate policy priorities and announce new measures. We summarize our key takeaways as below. 2. The PBOC plans to make the overnight reverse repo rate its main policy rate. Governor Pan noted that DR001 has effectively become the PBOC’s operational target for short-term interest rates, while the current main policy rate remains the 7-day reverse repo rate (Exhibit 1). To better align the policy rate with the operational target, the PBOC will study a transition towards overnight reverse repos as its main open market operation instrument, with the overnight OMO rate eventually replacing the 7-day reverse repo rate as the main policy rate. The announcement follows earlier reforms to the short-term interest rate corridor and the PBOC’s liquidity management toolkit. Higher yields have revived questions about whether the ECB will stop QT. This conflates balance sheet implementation, the monetary policy stance and fragmentation concerns. The current framework and money -market signals suggest that point remains some way off, while recent rhetoric continues to point to the policy rate as the main line of defence. When will the ECB stop QT? This has been increasingly asked in recent weeks prompted by the rise in yields globally, and more recently, the widening in OAT spreads. This conflates balance sheet implementation, the monetary policy stance and fragmentation concerns. Under the demand -driven framework outlined in 2024, the launch of the structural portfolio will occur only once the balance sheet starts to grow and after bank demand for the OMOs has risen substantially. The sequencing of events is particularly relevant. The implementation of the framework is separate from the monetary policy stance, which is set by the level of the policy rate. First, within any given OAD the OAS is widely dispersed, which tells us the obvious, which is that the market is not pricing to our modeled call: if it were, bonds with the same call outcome would cluster at a similar spread. Second, the cross-vintage pattern still makes directional sense. The 2023 vintage, very likely to be called, prints 0.5 year OADs and offers roughly 100-125bp of OAS. The 2024 vintage sits at 1-1.5 year OADs with a wider spread of OAS, the widest clustering in the 70-80 area. The 2025 and 2026 vintages extend to 2 to 4 year OADs with a similarly wide OAS distribution, and the 2021 and 2022 deals carry the longest OADs of all, with some trading at meaningfully negative OAS to modeled call. Keep in mind that OAS alone is a difficult number to realize, and OAS to modeled call is even tougher. This should be taken more as a relative value tool, letting us pick one bond over another. In summary, we see opportunities in non-QM. Our model sees limited risk of 2025 and 2026 deals extending to longer than a 5-year profile, with prepay speeds holding in the low double digits. For discounted bonds, that combination skews the risk to the upside, but some bonds screen better than others.

Global Equity Strategy 19 October 2026 ab 21 3. Add Utilities/Renewables exposure. US Utilities over US Staples (and Telecom). After correcting 15% from the Jul highs to the Sep lows, Utilities have had a small bounce in Oct. As rates have risen, Utilities P/E has fallen toward 15x, near 10+ year lows, despite rising medium-term EPS growth expectations on increased capex and power demand. While higher bond yields raise interest costs for Utilities on new financings for capex and existing bonds, they can usually recapture the increased interest cost in the allowed rate base. On the other side, Staples P/E is a lofty~25x, despite falling EPS growth potential. Telecom also screens near the bottom on REVS and has outperformed the ML implied moves, making it an attractive source of funds for Utilities as well. Utilities earnings yields plus EPS CAGR is nearly 16%, compared to just ~11% for Staples. Both are rates sensitive, but Utilities are also less crowded than Staples. In the case of bond yields normalizing some, we see investors reallocating back to Utilities given its higher growth is now at a big discount. China: Q3 GDP slightly beat expectations on broad-based improvement in September activity 19 October 2026 | 2:35PM HKT Bottom line: China’s Q3 GDP slightly beat market expectations, thanks to a broad-based improvement in September economic activity — especially retail sales and services industry output. The imbalance between strong exports and weak domestic final demand remained significant. Industrial production (IP) growth accelerated further to 5.5% yoy in September from 5.2% yoy in August, led by faster output growth in chemicals and non-metal product manufacturing industries. On a single-month basis, the year-on-year contraction in fixed asset investment (FAI) narrowed to -7.2% in September from -10.8% in August, thanks to more favorable weather and a low base. Retail sales growth rebounded to +1.1% yoy in September from +0.4% yoy in August, mainly led by offline goods sales and restaurant sales revenue, as the earlier Mid-Autumn Festival may have shifted some consumption from October into September. The Services Industry Output Index, reported in real terms and closely correlated with tertiary GDP growth, rebounded to 4.8% yoy in September from 4.1% yoy in August. Regardless of the outcome, continued deficit expansion and the resulting pressure on the long end matter more for refinancing conditions across our coverage. A divided government caps the odds of sweeping change in either direction, which limits policy shocks but equally limits relief. Companies with front-loaded maturities and thin liquidity carry that risk regardless of who wins. Well-laddered, deleveraging companies with strong FCF conversion should continue to do well through any configuration. The prioritization of the regularity of meeting dates against the timeliness of key data releases might seem suboptimal. As such, it makes sense to contemplate whether a better FOMC meeting calendar could be achieved. In our view, such considerations should account for the following priorities: 1. Data availability : Maximize the timeliness of key data availability (e.g., payrolls, CPI and PCE) while also allowing enough time between the release and meeting to fully incorporate the news. 2. Spacing: Keep meetings at a roughly equal distance across the calendar. 3. Avoidance of conflicts: Do not hold meetings on days that conflict with other key global central banks, including the ECB, BoE, and BoJ. 4. Liquidity: Avoid holidays and other dates/time periods that could have lower liquidity. Given these principles, there are endless possibilities for how to structure the 2027 calendar. We present three options. If the Fed wanted to pursue Warsh’s idea of six FOMC meetings, one possibility would be to hold those meetings on February 17, April 21, June 16, August 18, October 20, and December 15. records.text: Market backdrop Soren Willemann Barclays, UK Well ahead of the French presidential elections in April 2027, France grabbed headlines amid a sharp sell-off in OATs as large budget deficits gained market attention once more. This, coupled with oil prices above $100/bbl has led to a meaningful sell-off across credit, with €IG 14bp wider and €HY 80bp wider since our last Credit Risk Factor publication on 8 September. With €IG at 95bp, and €HY at 360bp, we are now wider than our base-case for end-2026 spreads (by 5bp and 43bp respectively). As we discussed in our latest European Credit Alpha, we see a backdrop of continued volatility with no near-term catalyst for a "resolution" to political uncertainty in France or the conflict in the Middle East. Thrown into the mix there has been a notable uptick in single-name volatility in HY. Though inherently idiosyncratic, the underlying driver of the majority of this volatility is higher financing costs and the associated impact on the viability of the companies. With this bearish backdrop, and the weather having turned decidedly autumnal, we should not lose sight of supportive factors: growth remains strong, with recession risk low, and a high savings rate, coupled with high yields should support demand for credit (once/if rate volatility subsides). records.text: ab 16 October 2026 Global Research US Economic Perspectives Midterms could shift fiscal and Fed policy Based on the most recent polling, the midterm elections are likely to increase Democratic control of Congress. Democrats need a net gain of three House seats, and the incumbent president's party has lost an average of 24 seats over the past 20 midterm cycles. A Democratic House would make gridlock and fiscal brinkmanship more likely; a Democratic sweep could also affect monetary policy through increased control of the Senate confirmation process. If the Democrats win control of the Senate, we would expect as many as four of the current members of the Board of Governors could depart in 2027 or by early 2028. Spillovers into monetary policymaking: an underappreciated risk A blue sweep could have implications for the Congressional confirmation process. Natural turnover in the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve gives the administration the ability to appoint new members. Those new members must go through a Congressional confirmation process. A Democratic majority could therefore constrain the administration’s ability to secure confirmation for its preferred nominees. Greater Democratic influence over confirmations, alongside increased oversight, could in turn provide the FOMC with a degree of additional institutional insulation. The result is an increasingly bifurcated picture: while current BDC marks do not point to broad-based technology impairment, weakness is becoming more visible in older vintages and selected software credits as they approach maturity. While the maturity wall does not itself create the underlying credit problem, refinancing may increasingly force price discovery where current marks prove difficult to sustain, driving greater dispersion in realized outcomes across portfolios. Conclusion: stress deferred, not defused In short, global private credit will face a more meaningful test from mid-2027, as rising technology maturities increasingly expose weaker vintages to refinancing at a point when earnings buffers are thin and capital may become more selective. Higher rates alone appear unlikely to drive broad-based stress; the bigger risk is that an earnings shock, particularly across software, coincides with rising refinancing needs across weaker vintages and turns today’s concentrated weakness into a broader credit problem. We expect dispersion to remain the defining feature of the next stage of the private-credit cycle, with refinancing outcomes increasingly separating stronger borrowers from weaker credits.

Robust exports, led by technology products, machinery and EVs, should help cushion the drag from sharply slowing investment and lackluster consumption. However, we expect another sub-4.5% yoy reading in Q3 (see: Sep data preview). Any potential rebound in sequential growth is more likely to emerge no earlier than in Q4, as the RMB800bn in structural lending tools deployed in late August and the recently announced additional issuance of RMB550bn local government bond begin to take effect. Policy support remains a step behind domestic weakness Despite domestic demand weakness, the stimulus gap continued to widen. In our view, this is partly due to policy makers’ higher tolerance level of lower growth, and partly still robust export growth at 20%+ (see China Viewpoint). However, three-month annualized CPI-Median and CPI-Trim inflation have increased to approximately 2.7% and 2.6%, respectively, from 2.3% and 2.2% in August. Taken together, the data suggest some persistence in core inflation, but do not yet establish a sustained acceleration. Inflation breadth reinforces the relatively narrow picture. Our bottom-up decomposition of 150 CPI categories indicates that around 32% of the basket is experiencing annual inflation above 3%, while roughly 28% is experiencing outright price declines. Around 31% of the basket is in categories where price pressures have accelerated relative to three months earlier, broadly matched by the share experiencing deceleration. Highlights this week The mood at the IMF/WB meetings in Bangkok was notably more cautious than it would have been a month ago (see here for a replay of our macro conference panels). Recent bond-market stress, particularly in Europe, had shifted the debate from resilience towards fragility, while the tech sell-off prompted questions about whether the AI trade had reached a turning point. We expect the euro-area composite PMI to ease to 52.8 from 53.1, with weakness concentrated in services, while manufacturing should remain broadly stable. records.text: US Economic Weekly | 16 October 2026 5 Assets: Homeownership stalled while stock holdings rose Turning to the asset side of household balance sheets, the 2025 SCF shows that overall homeownership rate declined between the 2022 and 2025 surveys (Exhibit 3). Housing affordability also remained near historical lows, with the median home worth more than 4.5 times median family income. This is consistent with the sharp rise in mortgage rates over this period. And, affordability pressures are unlikely to have improved materially this year given still-elevated borrowing costs and the Fed’s resumption of rate hikes in September. The picture for equities was somewhat different. Conditional on owning stocks, median stock holdings increased 36% between 2022 and 2025 as per SCF. However, stock- market participation edged down from 58% to 56%, though it remained above its 2019 level of 53% (Exhibit 4). The decline since 2022 was driven by families outside the top 10% of the income distribution. Conversely, an indifference to this tightening may invoke memories of Powell's 2018 "Auto-Pilot" remarks in reference to that tightening episode. • Where are we in the broader equity market correction? Equity and other risk markets have been correcting for over 3 months. We were early to identify this correction as a migration from early cycle to mid cycle at the same time the AI trade was transitioning from enablers to adopters. Key observations include the poor breadth of the market and a very distinct and now obvious outperformance of the quality factor noted above. The finality of such corrections typically end with the high quality index catching down even as the factor itself holds up. This can happen quickly or more slowly. Be ready either way as this will likely mark the end of the correction,

For US and EU private- credit technology, a 10% annualized decline in EBITDA would push the median ICR below 1.0x by late 2028. records.text: 2 Euro Area Watch | 16 October 2026 Paris fieldtrip notes The prospect of a 2027 budget deal, including almost 0.7ppt of primary budget adjustment, may give rating agencies a reason to sit on their hands until after the election. But the deficit will remain large, further adjustment still needed, and the post- 27 election policy choices pivotal, yet unknown. 2027 election: very strong choices on the menu The 2027 election featured prominently in all our discussions. A common theme was that the popular narrative and current polls might overstate the likelihood of a victory for far-right candidate Le Pen in the presidential election. Markets may at the same time underestimate the potential economic consequences at national and EU levels. Opinion polls show still low interest in the 2027 election among survey participants, although with higher mobilisation among the far left and far right. Past election cycles would suggest polls start to move in earnest in February-March as campaigns reach full throttle. In this particular cycle, the crowded field of candidates in the centre creates considerable space for polls to move, we heard. Uncertainty on parliamentary majorities was high, though we were surprised that most speakers seemed to see a path to a presidential majority of sorts in parliament. The US and UK are likely to maintain the highest term premium, given their recent track record of above-target inflation and lack of progress towards fiscal consolidation. In the Euro Area we think Bund scarcity is a thing of the past since the German debt brake was abolished, and EU institutional improvements have dampened sovereign risks while reducing the safe asset premium in Bunds. That said, a return to safe-haven dynamics in light of sovereign spread widening likely puts a ceiling above Bund yields, and we think once inflation risks recede Bund term premium has scope to decline. For Japan, exiting the era of ultra-easy monetary policy has reinvigorated right-tail risks, and rate expectations remain slow to adapt to this new regime. But we think it will take a stabilisation in rates expectations and greater clarity of the endpoint for monetary policy first for term premium to moderate. We view this degree of flatness as anomalous and an attractive opportunity in rates. Current market pricing implies that inflation will remain persistent enough to warrant higher policy rates in the near-term, yet also suggests rates will remain largely unchanged several years into the future. This combination appears difficult to reconcile and, as such, we see value in the intermediate sector of the curve, particularly the 2Y-5Y area or 2Yx2Y to benefit from the mispricing across the US, Euro Area and UK markets. The opportunity remains robust across inflation scenarios. Under a disinflationary outcome, central banks would eventually have less need to maintain restrictive policy settings, leading the intermediate sector pricing lower future rates. Conversely, if inflation proves more persistent, central banks may be forced to deliver a deeper and more front-loaded hiking cycle. In that scenario, the peak in policy rates would likely be reached sooner and be followed by a sharper normalization in rates than is currently reflected in forwards. Either way, the current flat structure appears difficult to justify fundamentally and leaves the intermediate sector well positioned across a range of inflation outcomes. When unveiling their forecasts, the IMF and the World Bank staff highlighted the UK as one DM country where fiscal consolidation is underway. This might appear surprising, although it echoes our take following last year’s Budget (see here and here). Between the IMF’s assessment, French fiscal headlines, and the upcoming UK Budget, we thought this week was a good moment to take stock of where the UK is on its consolidation path, and what challenges lie ahead. We estimate that the UK is running a primary deficit of ~1% of GDP in the current fiscal year (FY2026/27). This is a sizable drop from 2.4% recorded in FY2024/25 and 1.4% achieved FY2025/26. This reduction was attained largely through an increase in the tax burden, which we estimate has risen by ~2.5% of GDP since FY2024/25. As a share of nominal GDP, expenditure has risen over this period, with debt servicing costs alone, we estimate, rising by 0.3% of GDP. Consolidating fiscal balances can be undertaken through increases in the tax burden, or spending cuts – or, rather, real- term spending freezes, where nominal cash balances are not uprated in line with inflation. So far, the UK has achieved its consolidation through the tax lever. This, of course, means re-distributing private sector GVA into public sector GVA, insofar as a higher tax burden and higher interest rates act as a dampener on private sector activity, with the size of the state expanding. We have discussed why this interpretation is incomplete and see two main reasons why Spain can sustain its constructive growth trajectory. First, the economy is showing signs of a deeper structural shift towards high value-added services, which would benefit from political stability and a clearer, more predictable tax framework. Second, Spain’s fiscal outlook remains prudent, with the deficit projected below 2.5% of GDP in 2027 and a negative fiscal impulse indicating that fiscal policy has already turned contractionary as Recovery Fund support begins to fade and public investment growth slowed in 2025 (Exhibit 3). Despite these constructive fundamentals, Spanish yields have become increasingly correlated with French yields, in line with the broader co-movement among European sovereigns. Financial conditions have also tightened broadly in line with the euro area average (Exhibit 4). In our view, the strong economic performance and solid fiscal position of Spain are at odds with the cheapening of Spanish sovereign debt observed in the last two months. Meanwhile, following a widening in Q1, the monthly budget deficit (excluding RRF pre-financing) has improved markedly on a better composition of non-interest spending. Wage and services CPI dynamics have seen a steady improvement too, lending credibility to the central bank’s reduced inflation target of 2.5%, due to be implemented from January 2028. Furthermore, the positive ‘animal spirits’ that we had expected in the wake of the mid-April election result continue to take hold across the economy. There is growing evidence on both the supply and demand side that activity and investment is recovering. Domestic profitability is up too, alongside higher productivity, which is also helping to shield Hungary against rising external inflation pressures compared with its peers (see EM: Reflation risks beyond the war, dated 3 July). We therefore have renewed confidence in our forecast for Hungary’s economy to grow in excess of 3.5% in 2027 from an estimated 2.0% this year, and for the NBH to be in a position to resume a careful easing cycle (once external conditions allow). This stands out relative to what we observe in insurer and pension fund holdings. Fixed Maturity Funds: Fixed maturity products are a potential source of support. Assets remain close to their €235bn peak, but growth has been subdued despite yields having approached levels that underpinned the initial expansion of the fund universe. It is too early for the move to have translated into flows, but yields stabilising at elevated levels should support renewed growth. A key question for 2027 is reinvestment, as we estimate that €40bn will mature next year. Following the rise in yields, many investors should be able to reinvest at yields comparable to, or higher than, those available at inception. Our analysis indicates reinvestments look attractive even if yields were to moderate more meaningfully from current levels. records.text: US Rates Strategy 16 October 2026 Citi Research 2 The intraday swings in rates after this week’s CPI upside surprise can be viewed as a fitting foreshadow of how rates and curve could reprice over the medium term. The initial post-CPI knee-jerk spike in yields (Tsy 2y sold off as much as 16bps and the curve bear flattened) quickly reversed as risky assets sold off, with 10y and 30y ultimately rallying on the day and the yield curve bull flattening (Figure 1). The growing concerns around the AI growth outlook also fueled the flight-to-quality long-end rally on the day, which was essentially a partial reversal of the AI-driven real yield sell-off from the prior month (Figure 2). But today’s rates sell-off amid higher oil price is a quick reminder that the market has not settled on a consistent macro driver yet. While it is difficult to tell if the ongoing AI de-risking is going to lead to a sustained rate rally, the post-CPI price action is at least supportive of our view that in a meaningful growth slowdown, investors would still find Treasuries attractive as a “safe haven” asset, especially at these elevated yields. At the same time, further Fed tightening would incrementally increase the risk of a slowdown, and this self-correcting dynamic should favor flatter front-end 2s5s and SOFR curves, as we previously discussed (US Rates Weekly - Only hawks outside the window). Will the Selloff Trigger Fund Outflows? — Daily Lipper data suggests modest fund outflows last Friday and Tuesday, before the trend reversed with modest inflows on Wednesday. Our fund flow model currently projects stable inflows in October and November, even under a bear-case scenario where 10yr yields rise a further 20bp by month end. This suggests near-term redemption risk remains contained. Meanwhile, our positioning model estimates a 0.6-0.7% increase in MBS overweights in September and October, although the projection remains sensitive to MBS index and IG spread movements over the rest of the month. Risks to Foreign Demand Skew to the Downside — Private investors continue to drive foreign MBS demand. Recent Fed custody data and our analysis of the late 2023 selloff suggest limited risk of net selling by foreign investors during the sell- off. Nordic hydro levels have kept falling so far in October, with no signs of relief yet and the latest ECMWF seasonal forecast pushing a recovery in precipitation to December. Week 41 NO2 reservoir levels stood at 52.1%, 19pp below the five-year average of 71.1% and significantly below 2022 drought levels of 62.6%. French hydro faces a similar predicament, with hydro levels at a 10-year low of 47.8% in Week 41, 23pp below the seasonal normal, posing further upside risks to French power in winter. We also expect the UK and Germany to be impacted, given their exposure to European hydro imports. The 1.4GW UK–Norway link accounts for about 4% of UK’s winter demand, while Germany’s estimated interconnector capacity with Norway and Switzerland amounts to around 7GW, or 13% of its winter demand . Weak hydro effects to persist: We think it will be difficult for European hydro stocks to recover to five-year average levels even if El Niño leads to a wetter winter, which will weigh on hydro generation throughout 2027. First, less benign corrections coincide with sizeable foreign equity outflows; technical corrections do not. Second, KRW-KOSPI correlations can turn positive as risk-off overwhelms hedging flows. Third, KOSPI-VKOSPI correlations can turn negative as volatility rises with equity weakness; benign corrections show the opposite. On all three, the past fortnight looks less benign, although signals remain measured given the staggered decline. If the sell-off subsides, concerns should fade; accelerating foreign selling would weaken the hedge cushion. #3. Would a KOSPI recovery help KRW? For KRW, the pace matters. A gradual recovery could unwind foreign underweights (UBSe: >4ppt in benchmarks), with portfolio inflows outweighing dollar demand for rebuilding of FX hedges. We also expect questions about ECB plans to potentially raise the Minimum Reserve Requirement. As before, we expect the ECB to raise rates by 25bp to 2.75% on 17 December. Previously, we thought this would be the peak. However, after revising our Eurozone inflation forecast higher, with inflation now expected to peak at 4% or above in early 2027, we are adding another 25bp hike to 3.0% in March 2027. We expect the ECB to start reversing these hikes from Q1 2028, bringing the depo rate back to 2.25% - our estimate of neutral - by Q3 2028. We see no reason for the ECB to accelerate the pace of rate hikes So far, the ECB has hiked rates in a gradual fashion, in June and September, based on updated staff macroeconomic forecasts. Price volatility can have a significant impact on the relative weights in our GSTOT indices—one reason to use time-varying weights. We can see this clearly when we compare how gold import shares changed from 2023 to 2025 (Exhibit 2) following the rally in gold prices over that period (Exhibit 3). We then adjust the raw trade shares for the importance of commodities trade in an economy’s output using an updated GDP scaling factor that also reflects 2025 data. To minimize “double counting” of price deviations, we keep this output adjustment fixed and revise the full index history to incorporate the new scaling factor. In this year’s update we also implement two additional modifications. First, we introduce chain-linked indexing to preserve continuity in the series by minimizing level shifts arising from annual changes in weights. Second, we substitute “mirror data”— the sum of the trade data reported by all trading partners rather than the reporting country itself—for Switzerland’s gold exports and imports from 1998-2011 to improve data quality. The full set of weights are shown in the Appendix. Overall, the weights update leaves our GSTOT indices relatively little changed (Exhibit 4). The administration's Project Vault is a ~$12B domestic strategic stockpile for critical materials, funded largely by the Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM) with support from private sector capital. The stockpile serves as a commercial insurance mechanism and liquidity buffer so U.S. industrial companies (such as automotive, aerospace, and high-tech firms) can avoid severe production cuts or plant shutdowns during supply shocks. It is paired with a proposed preferential trade zone utilizing rigid price floors. A Republican hold would likely expand this framework, along with faster permitting and extraction from non-traditional sources (e.g., vanadium recovered from petroleum catalysts for steelmaking). Under a divided government, we expect the program to survive but potentially face closer scrutiny. Democratic lawmakers, led by figures like Senator Martin Heinrich (D-NM) and Representative Jared Huffman (D-CA), have formally requested investigations into executive-branch mining and mineral awards, focusing on alleged conflicts of interest. records.text: EUR: What could possibly go wrong. The Euro has found some relief from the n global rally in duration, and the earlier contagion in sovereign spreads has partly relaxed. Through the “ups” of August and “downs” of the last few weeks, we have maintained our forecasts for the Euro to trade around 1.12-1.14 over the coming year because we think solid global growth and broadly synchronized policy should translate to relatively limited FX spot returns, and European fundamentals today are very different to past episodes of EA sovereign credit stress. We still see some challenges ahead, but over the next few months clarity on natural gas reserves for winter and a firmer foothold from global duration on the back of cooling US inflation pressures should be tailwinds for the Euro. That said, we think FX investors are right to focus on the recent stresses in sovereign yields and explore the downside tail in the Euro. Sovereign spread widening is particularly negative for a currency because it can lead to both (i) a shift in the mix of tightening away from monetary policy (a lower path for the policy rate and lower-risk real yields), and (ii) reduced foreign investor appetite. We have argued that FX vol would reset higher if there are signs of rising recession risk or divergence, and sovereign credit stress activates both of these powerful channels. But there are other, harder-to-measure factors that could help explain the residual in our model. First, our model does not account for global spillovers. This is a modeling choice, but when we include an (instrumented) global term premium variable, the fit of the model improves. Second, the shift in global savings and investment due to AI capex could be putting upward pressure on term premium by raising the sensitivity of longer-term yields to sovereign debt supply and raising overall debt supply. Third, the succession of supply shocks since the pandemic has weakened the (positive) correlation between growth and inflation. In turn, this has eroded the hedge value of duration in a balanced portfolio, visible in the increase in the equity-bond price correlation, for which investors should require higher term premium to compensate (Exhibit 5). Under our baseline of inflation moderation, amidst so far limited second-round effects, we expect macro uncertainty to gradually decline as a source of term premium. However, greater certainty on the path for energy prices seems to be a prerequisite for this, and so far it remains elusive. Weighing these factors, the current schedule of eight meetings each year might still be considered adequate.” Towards a better calendar This historical perspective highlights that the current FOMC calendar was built around a monetary framework that no longer exists. It is, therefore, reasonable to consider whether a better calendar could be achieved that fits the Fed’s current framework and data/policy cycles. The current calendar has clear drawbacks. For example, it does not account for when key data are released. This often leaves the Fed with relatively stale data at each meeting. Look no further than the December FOMC meeting which occurs the day before the November CPI report. This is not an isola ted occurrence. PCE data – which provide the latest read on the Fed’s target inflation gauge -- were released within days after the April, July, and October meetings this year. In the past, CPI releases have also occurred in close enough proximity to the FOMC meeting that it was in question whether the data were fully reflected in the Fed’s decision, communications, and projections. The 2027 calendar faces similar issues. CPI releases are either during or just after the June, September, and December FOMC meetings. That window is open. The 5y has come back more than 10bp from 2.43% on September 28 to 2.33% on Wednesday, the auctions were clean, and inflation compensation has not budged. We would rebuild the paid belly in the forward fly (1y1y x 2y3y x 5y5y) primarily into the BoJ's October 29–30 hold confirmation. The 10y BEI widener (recommended September 10 at 1.95% on our marks, target 2.25%, stop 1.75%) has tracked from 2.02% to 2.17% on the generic BEI, up 15bp; if the target comes into reach before the BoJ meeting, take profit mechanically. The 5y range stays at 2.30–2.50% — a hawkish FOMC backdrop after the CPI surprise should keep the bottom of the range intact. For the 20y we assume 3.75–4.00% for now; if the sector settles into the lower half of that range after the auction, the super-long trade is to own the carry. Within that trade, the +14bp dislocation around the 25-year point in Figure 6 is worth harvesting by switching part of a 20y take-up into the old 30y issues in that zone. Shoki Omori

Equally, in a divided Congress the policy agenda would be driven by areas with most scope for bipartisanship.
